papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: On the Bias Against Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: How do inductive biases affect the performance of small to moderately-sized isotropic networks in unsupervised visual feature learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that inductive biases, such as locality in convolutions and distance preservation in continuous input encodings, significantly benefit small-scale isotropic networks for unsupervised visual learning, contrasting with large-scale models where these biases are removed.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that small-scale isotropic networks benefit from inductive biases, and improvements in small-scale models may transfer to large-scale models, enabling broader research participation.
papers.key_findings:
Convolutional networks outperform MLP-mixer and transformer networks in both unsupervised and classification tasks.
Continuous input encoding yields the best classification accuracy for a fixed unsupervised loss.
There is a strong correlation between unsupervised generative model performance and downstream classification accuracy.
Transformer models perform poorly on small-scale problems compared to convolutional and MLP-mixer models.
Different input encodings pair better with specific architecture types, suggesting untested inductive biases.
papers.limitation:
Limited computing resources prevent determining if poor transformer performance is due to data or architecture.
Linear probes were trained on isolated layers rather than combinations, which may not capture best features.
future_direction: Exploring linear probes on combinations of layers rather than isolated layers.
Investigating untested inductive biases that may improve large-scale isotropic networks.
papers.abstract: Borrowing from the transformer models that revolutionized the field of natural language processing, self-supervised feature learning for visual tasks has also seen state-of-the-art success using these extremely deep, isotropic networks. However, the typical AI researcher does not have the resources to evaluate, let alone train, a model with several billion parameters and quadratic self-attention activations. To facilitate further research, it is necessary to understand the features of these huge transformer models that can be adequately studied by the typical researcher. One interesting characteristic of these transformer models is that they remove most of the inductive biases present in classical convolutional networks. In this work, we analyze the effect of these and more inductive biases on small to moderately-sized isotropic networks used for unsupervised visual feature learning and show that their removal is not always ideal.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: ExpPoint-MAE: Better Interpretability and Performance for Self-Supervised Point Cloud Transformers
papers.research_question: What are the properties of transformers attained through self-supervision in the point cloud domain, and how effective are Masked Autoencoding and Momentum Contrast as pretraining schemes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a strategic unfreezing finetuning strategy that improves classification accuracy by retaining pretrained features, and adapts explainability tools to analyze self-supervised point cloud transformers.
papers.conclusion: The proposed unfreezing strategy improves model performance by preserving useful pretrained features, and explainability analysis reveals that self-supervised pretraining enables transformers to learn meaningful geometric representations in point clouds.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed strategic unfreezing strategy consistently outperforms the baseline, achieving state-of-the-art classification results among transformer models on ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN.
With more pretraining data, the transformer learns to attend locally in early layers and globally in later layers, mimicking a convolutional inductive bias.
Pretrained models attend to semantically meaningful regions of point clouds, indicating a better understanding of underlying geometry, while models without pretraining do not.
Masked Autoencoding (MAE) pretraining outperforms Momentum Contrast (MoCo) pretraining for point cloud transformers in classification tasks.
The transformer can reconstruct point clouds even with very high masking ratios (e.g., 90%), and intermediate layers contain sufficient information for classification.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve into the properties of transformers, attained through self-supervision, in the point cloud domain. Specifically, we evaluate the effectiveness of Masked Autoencoding as a pretraining scheme, and explore Momentum Contrast as an alternative. In our study we investigate the impact of data quantity on the learned features, and uncover similarities in the transformer’s behavior across domains. Through comprehensive visualizations, we observe that the transformer learns to attend to semantically meaningful regions, indicating that pretraining leads to a better understanding of the underlying geometry. Moreover, we examine the finetuning process and its effect on the learned representations. Based on that, we devise an unfreezing strategy which consistently outperforms our baseline without introducing any other modifications to the model or the training pipeline, and achieve state-of-the-art results in the classification task among transformer models.

papers.title: Transformers self-organize like newborn visual systems when trained in prenatal worlds
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn like brains? Specifically, do transformers develop the same structure as newborn visual systems when exposed to the same prenatal sensory experiences (retinal waves)?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on prenatal retinal waves spontaneously develop the same structural signatures as newborn visual systems (edge sensitivity in early layers, shape sensitivity in later layers, and increasing receptive field sizes), suggesting that brains and transformers learn via common space-time fitting principles.
papers.conclusion: Transformers spontaneously develop the same structure as newborn visual systems when trained on prenatal retinal waves, indicating that brains and transformers learn in common ways via general space-time fitting principles.
papers.key_findings:
After training on retinal waves, transformers develop oriented edge sensitivity in early layers.
After training on retinal waves, transformers develop shape sensitivity in later layers, prioritizing object contours over color.
After training on retinal waves, transformers develop progressively larger receptive field sizes across layers, mimicking hierarchical and retinotopic organization.
Temporal scrambling of the retinal wave input prevents the development of edge sensitivity, shape sensitivity, and increasing receptive field sizes.
The development of these structural signatures becomes more robust with increasing amounts of retinal wave training data.
papers.limitation:
Only three key signatures of newborn visual systems were tested; other characteristics could be explored.
Only one unsupervised temporal learning objective was used; alternative objectives might produce different organizational structures.
Only prenatal visual experiences were simulated; other modalities (auditory, proprioceptive, tactile) were not explored.
future_direction: Explore whether other characteristics of visual systems develop spontaneously when space-time fitting transformers adapt to prenatal experience.
Test whether transformers equipped with alternative unsupervised temporal learning objectives also self-organize like newborn visual systems.
Simulate prenatal input in other domains, including auditory, proprioceptive, and tactile experiences.
papers.abstract: Do transformers learn like brains? A key challenge in addressing this question is that transformers and brains are trained on fundamentally different data. Brains are initially "trained" on prenatal sensory experiences (e.g., retinal waves), whereas transformers are typically trained on large datasets that are not biologically plausible. We reasoned that if transformers learn like brains, then they should develop the same structure as newborn brains when exposed to the same prenatal data. To test this prediction, we simulated prenatal visual input using a retinal wave generator. Then, using self-supervised temporal learning, we trained transformers to adapt to those retinal waves. During training, the transformers spontaneously developed the same structure as newborn visual systems: (1) early layers became sensitive to edges, (2) later layers became sensitive to shapes, and (3) the models developed larger receptive fields across layers. The organization of newborn visual systems emerges spontaneously when transformers adapt to a prenatal visual world. This developmental convergence suggests that brains and transformers learn in common ways and follow the same general fitting principles.

papers.title: Decoding Vision Transformers: the Diffusion Steering Lens
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the direct contributions of individual submodules in Vision Transformers to understand their internal processing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Diffusion Steering Lens (DSL), a training-free method to visualize direct submodule contributions in Vision Transformers by steering representations and patching subsequent outputs.
papers.conclusion: DSL is a reliable method for visualizing direct submodule contributions in Vision Transformers, overcoming limitations of Diffusion Lens.
papers.key_findings:
Diffusion Steering Lens (DSL) effectively visualizes direct contributions of submodules like attention heads in Vision Transformers.
DSL reveals that earlier attention heads (e.g., L36H4) contribute to the final prediction, which Diffusion Lens fails to capture.
Ablating attention heads with DSL visualizations similar to the input image causes a larger loss in output cosine similarity, validating DSL's reliability.
DSL ablation strategies for removing synthetic overlays from images perform nearly as well as optimal ACDC-like ablation and better than random ablation.
Diffusion Lens visualizes residual stream representations but is insufficient for isolating direct submodule contributions.
papers.limitation: The steering operation may inadvertently alter representation content, and the diffusion-based decoder can introduce artifacts.
future_direction: Explore the visualization of image tokens for understanding early-layer processing.
Validate consistency with text-based methods.
Extend DSL to models without pretrained diffusion decoders.
papers.abstract: Logit Lens is a widely adopted method for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based language models, enabling the analysis of how internal representations evolve across layers by projecting them into the output vocabulary space. Although applying Logit Lens to Vision Transformers (ViTs) is technically straightforward, its direct use faces limitations in capturing the richness of visual representations. Building on the work of Toker et al. (2024)~\cite{Toker2024-ve}, who introduced Diffusion Lens to visualize intermediate representations in the text encoders of text-to-image diffusion models, we demonstrate that while Diffusion Lens can effectively visualize residual stream representations in image encoders, it fails to capture the direct contributions of individual submodules. To overcome this limitation, we propose \textbf{Diffusion Steering Lens} (DSL), a novel, training-free approach that steers submodule outputs and patches subsequent indirect contributions. We validate our method through interventional studies, showing that DSL provides an intuitive and reliable interpretation of the internal processing in ViTs.

papers.title: Sparse autoencoders reveal selective remapping of visual concepts during adaptation
papers.research_question: How do prompt-based adaptation techniques change the association of model inputs to interpretable concepts in CLIP, and does adaptation activate new concepts or reuse existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PatchSAE, a sparse autoencoder for vision transformers that provides spatial attribution of interpretable concepts, and finds that prompt-based adaptation improves performance primarily by adding new mappings between existing concepts and downstream classes, rather than activating new concepts.
papers.conclusion: PatchSAE is an effective tool for interpreting vision transformers, and prompt-based adaptation methods like MaPLe work by remapping existing visual concepts to new class labels rather than learning fundamentally new concepts.
papers.key_findings:
PatchSAE identifies diverse interpretable concepts (from simple visual patterns to high-level semantics) and provides spatial attribution of these concepts in images.
SAE latents contain class discriminative information, as ablating top-activating latents per class significantly reduces classification accuracy.
Prompt-based adaptation (MaPLe) and the original CLIP model activate a highly overlapping set of SAE latents, indicating similar concepts are recognized.
The performance gain from adaptation stems from tailoring the mapping between commonly activated concepts and downstream task classes, not from firing additional class-discriminative concepts.
PatchSAE trained on CLIP generalizes to the adapted model MaPLe, allowing comparison in a shared latent space.
papers.limitation: The scope of this work focuses on the CLIP vision encoder. Analysis of different vision encoders and joint analysis of multimodality could provide more comprehensive understanding.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to different vision encoders.
Jointly analyzing the multimodality of vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Adapting foundation models for specific purposes has become a standard approach to build machine learning systems for downstream applications. Yet, it is an open question which mechanisms take place during adaptation. Here we develop a new Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) for the CLIP vision transformer, named PatchSAE, to extract interpretable concepts at granular levels (e.g., shape, color, or semantics of an object) and their patch-wise spatial attributions. We explore how these concepts influence the model output in downstream image classification tasks and investigate how recent state-of-the-art prompt-based adaptation techniques change the association of model inputs to these concepts. While activations of concepts slightly change between adapted and non-adapted models, we find that the majority of gains on common adaptation tasks can be explained with the existing concepts already present in the non-adapted foundation model. This work provides a concrete framework to train and use SAEs for Vision Transformers and provides insights into explaining adaptation mechanisms.

papers.title: Interpretability of artificial neural network models in artificial Intelligence vs. neuroscience
papers.research_question: What are the different notions of interpretability in artificial intelligence and neuroscience, and how can neuroscientific interpretability be pursued independently?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that interpretability in AI and neuroscience are distinct, with neuroscientific interpretability requiring alignment between model components and brain constructs, and proposes that brain alignment can serve as a benchmark for evaluating AI explainability methods.
papers.conclusion: The authors encourage researchers to conceptually separate the objectives of AI and neuroscience interpretability, but suggest that AI interpretability methods aligned with primate brain interpretations are more promising.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-faceted construct used differently in AI (focusing on model component contributions to output) and neuroscience (requiring alignment with brain constructs).
Neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs is relative and depends on the model's intended use and the grain of analysis, with no need for full brain alignment if only specific experimental variables are of interest.
Current ANN models of primate vision contain features not mapped to neuroscientific constructs, limiting their neuroscientific interpretability.
Brain alignment (similarity with primate behavior and neural measurements) can validate the 'goodness' of AI explainability methods in the absence of ground truth.
AI interpretability methods that provide more primate-brain-aligned model interpretations are likely more promising, despite operational differences from brains.
papers.abstract: Computationally explicit hypotheses of brain function derived from machine learning (ML)-based models have recently revolutionized neuroscience. Despite the unprecedented ability of these artificial neural networks (ANNs) to capture responses in biological neural networks (brains), and our full access to all internal model components (unlike the brain), ANNs are often referred to as black-boxes with limited interpretability. Interpretability, however, is a multi-faceted construct that is used differently across fields. In particular, interpretability, or explainability, efforts in Artificial Intelligence (AI) focus on understanding how different model components contribute to its output (i.e., decision making). In contrast, the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs requires explicit alignment between model components and neuroscientific constructs (e.g., different brain areas or phenomena, like recurrence or top-down feedback). Given the widespread calls to improve the interpretability of AI systems, we here highlight these different notions of interpretability and argue that the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs can be pursued in parallel with, but independently from, the ongoing efforts in AI. Certain ML techniques (e.g., deep dream) can be leveraged in both fields, to ask what stimulus optimally activates the specific model features (feature visualization by optimization), or how different features contribute to the model's output (feature attribution). However, without appropriate brain alignment, certain features will remain uninterpretable to neuroscientists.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
papers.research_question: How do different inductive biases (architecture, task objective, visual training diet) affect the emergent brain alignment of learned visual representations in artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Visual training diet (dataset diversity) has the largest effect on brain predictivity, while architecture and task objective have smaller effects when controlled; many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity despite different representations, suggesting standard linking methods may be too flexible.
papers.conclusion: Dataset diversity is a key factor in developing brain-aligned visual representations, and current model-to-brain linking methods may need to be refined to better capture representational differences.
papers.key_findings:
CNN and transformer architectures achieve near equivalent brain predictivity when trained on the same dataset and task.
Instance-level contrastive learning objectives lead to more brain-predictive representations than non-contrastive self-supervised objectives.
Vision-language alignment (e.g., CLIP) does not consistently yield higher brain predictivity compared to purely visual contrastive learning when controlling for dataset.
Visual training diet (dataset diversity) has the largest effect on brain predictivity, with models trained on more diverse datasets (e.g., OpenAI's 400M dataset) performing best.
Many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity after feature re-weighting, suggesting that standard linking methods may be too flexible to capture representational differences.
papers.limitation: The two linking methods (classical RSA and voxel-encoding RSA) give different estimates of explained variance, and it is unclear which is more correct.
future_direction: Developing better metrics for dataset diversity and richness.
Refining model-to-brain linking methods to be less flexible and more diagnostic.
Exploring one-to-one mappings between model units and brain neurons, and expanding brain targets to include topographic organization.
papers.abstract: The rapid release of high-performing computer vision models offers new potential to study the impact of different inductive biases on the emergent brain alignment of learned representations. Here, we perform controlled comparisons among a curated set of 224 diverse models to test the impact of specific model properties on visual brain predictivity - a process requiring over 1.8 billion regressions and 50.3 thousand representational similarity analyses. We find that models with qualitatively different architectures (e.g. CNNs versus Transformers) and task objectives (e.g. purely visual contrastive learning versus vision- language alignment) achieve near equivalent brain predictivity, when other factors are held constant. Instead, variation across visual training diets yields the largest, most consistent effect on brain predictivity. Many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity, despite clear variation in their underlying representations - suggesting that standard methods used to link models to brains may be too flexible. Broadly, these findings challenge common assumptions about the factors underlying emergent brain alignment, and outline how we can leverage controlled model comparison to probe the common computational principles underlying biological and artificial visual systems.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: What can attribution methods show us about chemical language models?
papers.research_question: How can attribution methods be used to explain the predictions of a chemical language model for aqueous solubility?
papers.core_contribution: The adapted transformer-specific attribution method produces sparse attributions that reflect how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, while SHAP provides sensible atom-level attributions but fails to explain functional groups relevant to solubility.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods provide insight into how chemical language models represent molecules, but current techniques have limitations in explaining solubility predictions in terms of functional groups, instead revealing how the model organizes its latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning the MegaMolBART encoder significantly improves aqueous solubility prediction accuracy.
The transformer-specific attribution method (using the hRi token) yields sparse attributions that are characteristic of how the model represents molecular similarity in its latent space.
SHAP provides chemically sensible attributions (e.g., highlighting electronegative atoms) but does not explain predictions at the level of functional groups.
The fine-tuned model's latent space becomes linearly separable with respect to solubility along the first principal component.
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, limiting its ability to attribute negative contributions to solubility.
papers.limitation:
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, preventing attribution of features that negatively contribute to solubility.
SHAP does not capture functional group-level explanations for solubility predictions.
ECFP-based models are less predictive and their explanations are coarse-grained.
future_direction: Using the attributions to design focused, informative chemical datasets by creating training examples that contravene the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Language models trained on molecular string representations have shown strong performance in predictive and generative tasks. However, practical applications require not only making accurate predictions, but also explainability - the ability to explain the reasons and rationale behind the predictions. In this work, we explore explainability for a chemical language model by adapting a transformer-specific and a model-agnostic input attribution technique. We fine-tune a pretrained model to predict aqueous solubility, compare training and architecture variants, and evaluate visualizations of attributed relevance. The model-agnostic SHAP technique provides sensible attributions, highlighting the positive influence of individual electronegative atoms, but does not explain the model in terms of functional groups or explain how the model represents molecular strings internally to make predictions. In contrast, the adapted transformer-specific explainability technique produces sparse attributions, which cannot be directly attributed to functional groups relevant to solubility. Instead, the attributions are more characteristic of how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, which seems to represent features relevant to molecular similarity rather than functional groups. These findings provide insight into the representations underpinning chemical language models, which we propose may be leveraged for the design of informative chemical spaces for training more accurate, advanced and explainable models.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: What kinds of abstractions are learned by neurons in deep models? Do compositional explanations give insight into model performance? Can they be used to predictably manipulate model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a procedure for generating compositional logical explanations of individual neurons, which provides more precise and expressive characterizations of neuron behavior than atomic labels, and applies it to analyze vision and NLP models.
papers.conclusion: Compositional explanations offer a more precise and expressive way to characterize neuron behavior, providing insights into model performance and enabling targeted adversarial manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons learn compositional concepts: in image classification, some learn meaningful perceptual abstractions while others are polysemantic; in NLI, shallow heuristics (e.g., based on gender, lexical overlap) are reified in individual neurons.
The interpretability of neurons correlates differently with performance: in image classification, human-interpretable abstractions are positively correlated with accuracy, while in NLI, neurons explained by shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with accuracy.
Compositional explanations enable the creation of simple 'copy-paste' adversarial examples that predictably change model behavior by targeting specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
The method requires technical expertise to implement, limiting usability by non-experts.
It relies on annotated datasets which may be expensive to collect and may be biased in the features they contain or omit.
Neuron-level explanations cannot identify concepts distributed across multiple neurons or establish definitive causal chains between inputs and decisions.
future_direction: Building easier user interfaces for explainability.
Reducing data annotation requirements.
Extending composition operators (e.g., to relations like ABOVE and BELOW) and applying the method to other tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We describe a procedure for explaining neurons in deep representations by identifying compositional logical concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. Compared to prior work that uses atomic labels as explanations, analyzing neurons compositionally allows us to more precisely and expressively characterize their behavior. We use this procedure to answer several questions on interpretability in models for vision and natural language processing. First, we examine the kinds of abstractions learned by neurons. In image classification, we find that many neurons learn highly abstract but semantically coherent visual concepts, while other polysemantic neurons detect multiple unrelated features; in natural language inference (NLI), neurons learn shallow lexical heuristics from dataset biases. Second, we see whether compositional explanations give us insight into model performance: vision neurons that detect human-interpretable concepts are positively correlated with task performance, while NLI neurons that fire for shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with task performance. Finally, we show how compositional explanations provide an accessible way for end users to produce simple "copy-paste" adversarial examples that change model behavior in predictable ways.

papers.title: Multiscale Feature Attribution for Outliers
papers.research_question: What features render an input anomalous in outlier detection, particularly when anomalous test data exceed the limits of training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Inverse Multiscale Occlusion (IMO), a feature attribution method for outliers that uses inverse occlusion with multiple window sizes and baselines to identify anomalous features at various scales.
papers.conclusion: Inverse Multiscale Occlusion effectively identifies anomalous features in outliers, providing interpretable, scale-dependent attributions that outperform existing gradient-based and perturbative methods.
papers.key_findings:
IMO detects both large-scale anomalies (e.g., calibration offsets) and small-scale features (e.g., double-peaked emission lines) in spectroscopic outliers.
IMO outperforms gradient-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients and Expected Gradients, which often miss broad anomalies.
Inverse occlusion avoids issues with anomalous inputs by occluding baseline spectra with input segments, leading to more robust attributions.
Using multiple window sizes allows IMO to capture features at different scales without prior knowledge of feature size.
An ensemble of baselines with redshift adjustment improves attribution accuracy for astronomical spectra.
papers.abstract: Machine learning techniques can automatically identify outliers in massive datasets, much faster and more reproducible than human inspection ever could. But finding such outliers immediately leads to the question: which features render this input anomalous? We propose a new feature attribution method, Inverse Multiscale Occlusion, that is specifically designed for outliers, for which we have little knowledge of the type of features we want to identify and expect that the model performance is questionable because anomalous test data likely exceed the limits of the training data. We demonstrate our method on outliers detected in galaxy spectra from the Dark Energy Survey Instrument and find its results to be much more interpretable than alternative attribution approaches.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Generalizing biological surround suppression based on center surround similarity via deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do feedforward deep convolutional neural networks exhibit and generalize surround suppression effects based on center-surround similarity, and how do they compare to biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that feedforward convolutional neural networks exhibit surround suppression based on center-surround similarity, similar to biological V1 neurons, and introduces a gradient-based visualization method to generalize these effects to complex stimuli.
papers.conclusion: The findings generalize surround suppression to complex stimuli, providing testable hypotheses for higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach offers a new paradigm for biological experiments.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs show that the most suppressive surround orientation matches the center orientation, akin to V1 neurons.
Visualization reveals that for complex stimuli, the most suppressive surround is visually similar to the center.
In late layers, the most suppressive surround can follow changes in the center stimulus.
These effects are not present in untrained networks, indicating the role of learning.
Mismatches with biology include lack of geometric dependency in surround suppression and differences in contrast effects.
papers.limitation:
Feedforward CNNs lack clear center-surround separation and do not capture all biological surround effects, such as geometric dependencies.
CNNs show mismatches in contrast-dependent effects compared to cortical neurons.
future_direction: Elucidating the abstract mathematical form of surround effects in CNNs.
Incorporating scene statistics and divisive normalization into deep neural networks.
Testing hypotheses about efficient coding and high-order spatial dependencies.
papers.abstract: Sensory perception is dramatically influenced by the context. Models of contextual neural surround effects in vision have mostly accounted for Primary Visual Cortex (V1) data, via nonlinear computations such as divisive normalization. However, surround effects are not well understood within a hierarchy, for neurons with more complex stimulus selectivity beyond V1. We utilized feedforward deep convolutional neural networks and developed a gradient-based technique to visualize the most suppressive and excitatory surround. We found that deep neural networks exhibited a key signature of surround effects in V1, highlighting center stimuli that visually stand out from the surround and suppressing responses when the surround stimulus is similar to the center. We found that in some neurons, especially in late layers, when the center stimulus was altered, the most suppressive surround surprisingly can follow the change. Through the visualization approach, we generalized previous understanding of surround effects to more complex stimuli, in ways that have not been revealed in visual cortices. In contrast, the suppression based on center surround similarity was not observed in an untrained network. We identified further successes and mismatches of the feedforward CNNs to the biology. Our results provide a testable hypothesis of surround effects in higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach could be adopted in future biological experimental designs.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: Scaling MLPs: A Tale of Inductive Bias
papers.research_question: Do MLPs reflect the empirical advances exhibited by practical models, and can the lack of inductive bias in MLPs be compensated by scaling compute?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that MLPs, despite lacking vision-specific inductive bias, can achieve strong performance on image classification tasks when scaled in terms of compute, parameters, and data, and they exhibit predictable power-law scaling similar to modern architectures.
papers.conclusion: Lack of inductive bias in MLPs can be compensated by scale, and MLPs largely serve as a good proxy for modern architectures in terms of scaling behavior, though the roles of data augmentation and SGD implicit bias differ.
papers.key_findings:
MLP performance improves predictably as a power law with scale (compute, parameters, data).
Data augmentation is crucial for MLPs, acting as a necessary regularizer and source of inductive bias.
Contrary to CNNs, larger batch sizes improve generalization for MLPs.
Compute-optimal MLPs invest more compute into dataset size than model size compared to transformers.
MLPs achieve competitive results (e.g., 95% on CIFAR10, 82% on CIFAR100, 58% on ImageNet ReaL) with sufficient scale and augmentation.
papers.limitation:
MLPs struggle with fine-grained class distinctions and object localization, especially on complex datasets like ImageNet.
The scale employed may not be sufficient to fully test the hypothesis that less inductive bias is better at extremely large scales.
future_direction: Subjecting MLPs to even larger amounts of compute, especially in the form of more training examples.
papers.abstract: In this work we revisit the most fundamental building block in deep learning, the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), and study the limits of its performance on vision tasks. Empirical insights into MLPs are important for multiple reasons. (1) Given the recent narrative "less inductive bias is better", popularized due to transformers eclipsing convolutional models, it is natural to explore the limits of this hypothesis. To that end, MLPs offer an ideal test bed, as they lack any vision-specific inductive bias. (2) MLPs have almost exclusively been the main protagonist in the deep learning theory literature due to their mathematical simplicity, serving as a proxy to explain empirical phenomena observed for more complex architectures. Surprisingly, experimental datapoints for MLPs are very difficult to find in the literature, especially when coupled with large pre-training protocols. This discrepancy between practice and theory is worrying: Do MLPs reflect the empirical advances exhibited by practical models? Or do theorists need to rethink the role of MLPs as a proxy? We provide insights into both these aspects. We show that the performance of MLPs drastically improves with scale (95% on CIFAR10, 82% on CIFAR100, 58% on ImageNet ReaL), highlighting that lack of inductive bias can indeed be compensated. We observe that MLPs mimic the behaviour of their modern counterparts faithfully, with some components in the learning setting however exhibiting stronger or unexpected behaviours. Due to their inherent computational efficiency, large pre-training experiments become more accessible for academic researchers. All of our experiments were run on a single GPU.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Why Linear Interpretability Works: Invariant Subspaces as a Result of Architectural Constraints
papers.research_question: Why do linear interpretability methods like linear probes and sparse autoencoders succeed in deep nonlinear transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear interpretability methods succeed because transformer architectures have linear communication interfaces (attention OV circuits and unembedding matrices), which force semantic features to occupy context-invariant linear subspaces.
