It introduces the Self-Reference Property, where tokens provide the geometric directions for their associated features, enabling zero-shot semantic classification.
papers.conclusion: Linear interpretability in transformers is a structural consequence of architectural constraints, not merely an empirical regularity. The Self-Reference Property enables zero-shot semantic classification without labeled data.
papers.key_findings:
The Invariant Subspace Necessity theorem establishes that any semantic feature decoded through a linear interface must lie in a context-invariant subspace.
The Self-Reference Property shows that tokens directly provide the invariant geometric directions for their associated features.
Empirical validation across eight classification tasks and four model families confirms that class tokens align with instance directions, supporting directional invariance.
Zero-shot, unsupervised, and sparse autoencoder-based probes all recover the same directional structure, providing converging evidence.
Polysemy (one token with multiple directions) and partial synonymy (multiple tokens sharing a direction) are two sides of the same coin in the geometric representation.
papers.limitation:
The framework focuses on features communicated through linear interfaces; features operating through nonlinear gating (e.g., QK routing) may not exhibit the same invariance.
The work does not characterize when invariant subspaces collapse to single directions versus higher-dimensional structures.
future_direction: The Self-Reference Property suggests paths toward scalable, unsupervised circuit discovery.
The connection between sparse autoencoder features and token directions offers new evaluation criteria for dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Linear probes and sparse autoencoders consistently recover meaningful structure from transformer representations -- yet why should such simple methods succeed in deep, nonlinear systems? We show this is not merely an empirical regularity but a consequence of architectural necessity: transformers communicate information through linear interfaces (attention OV circuits, unembedding matrices), and any semantic feature decoded through such an interface must occupy a context-invariant linear subspace. We formalize this as the \emph{Invariant Subspace Necessity} theorem and derive the \emph{Self-Reference Property}: tokens directly provide the geometric direction for their associated features, enabling zero-shot identification of semantic structure without labeled data or learned probes. Empirical validation in eight classification tasks and four model families confirms the alignment between class tokens and semantically related instances. Our framework provides \textbf{a principled architectural explanation} for why linear interpretability methods work, unifying linear probes and sparse autoencoders.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: Can a simple method based on attribution patching outperform existing automated circuit discovery techniques in identifying important subnetworks (circuits) within neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP), a method that uses a linear approximation of activation patching via gradients, outperforms existing automated circuit discovery methods (like ACDC) in recovering known circuits while being significantly more computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms ACDC in identifying circuits while being substantially faster, though running ACDC on the subnetwork found by EAP can further improve results.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) achieves higher AUC for circuit recovery than ACDC on the IOI and Greater-Than tasks.
EAP is computationally efficient, requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass, unlike ACDC which scales exponentially with the number of nodes.
The linear approximation used in attribution patching can be inaccurate (e.g., concave curves) and may overestimate the effect of ablating an edge.
Running ACDC on the subgraph pruned by EAP can improve circuit identification performance over using EAP alone.
Attribution scores for edges in known circuits (e.g., name movers in IOI) align with their intuitive function, validating the method's outputs.
papers.limitation:
The metrics used for interpretability (like recovery of human-found circuits) do not precisely capture meaningful human understanding.
Human-found circuits are imperfect, which adds noise to the evaluation metric.
The linear approximation in attribution patching can be inaccurate, particularly for edges involving model embeddings, leading to overestimation of edge importance.
future_direction: Future circuit discovery experiments should run EAP first and then apply ACDC on the pruned subgraph.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability research has recently attracted attention as a potential research direction that could scale explanations of neural network behavior to large models. Existing automated circuit discovery work applies activation patching to identify subnetworks responsible for solving specific tasks (circuits). In this work, we show that a simple method based on attribution patching outperforms all existing methods while requiring just two forward passes and a backward pass. We apply a linear approximation to activation patching to estimate the importance of each edge in the computational subgraph. Using this approximation, we prune the least important edges of the network. We survey the performance and limitations of this method, finding that averaged over all tasks our method has greater AUC from circuit recovery than other methods.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: Data-driven emergence of convolutional structure in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can fully-connected neural networks learn convolutional structure directly from translation-invariant data, and what conditions drive the emergence of localized, space-tiling receptive fields?
papers.core_contribution: Fully-connected neural networks can learn convolutional structure (localized, space-tiling receptive fields) directly from translation-invariant data with non-Gaussian higher-order statistics, and this emergence is driven by higher-order correlations.
papers.conclusion: Higher-order statistics in translation-invariant data drive the emergence of convolutional structure in fully-connected neural networks, providing a new perspective on the development of low-level feature detectors.
papers.key_findings:
Fully-connected networks develop localized receptive fields when trained on non-Gaussian translation-invariant data, but not on Gaussian data with the same covariance.
The localized receptive fields tile the input space and resemble filters learned by convolutional networks trained on the same task.
The emergence of receptive fields is linked to tensor decomposition of higher-order input correlations, specifically the fourth-order cumulant.
Existing Gaussian theories of learning break down when receptive fields form, indicating the importance of non-Gaussian statistics.
The network learns higher-order statistics sequentially, with receptive field formation coinciding with a decrease in the excess kurtosis of pre-activations.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic data model and a simple two-layer network, limiting generalizability to more complex architectures and real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper architectures and recurrent networks.
Generalizing to other symmetry groups and understanding the conditions for learning invariances.
Studying the minimal amount of data necessary to detect such invariances.
papers.abstract: Exploiting data invariances is crucial for efficient learning in both artificial and biological neural circuits. Understanding how neural networks can discover appropriate representations capable of harnessing the underlying symmetries of their inputs is thus crucial in machine learning and neuroscience. Convolutional neural networks, for example, were designed to exploit translation symmetry and their capabilities triggered the first wave of deep learning successes. However, learning convolutions directly from translation-invariant data with a fully-connected network has so far proven elusive. Here, we show how initially fully-connected neural networks solving a discrimination task can learn a convolutional structure directly from their inputs, resulting in localised, space-tiling receptive fields. These receptive fields match the filters of a convolutional network trained on the same task. By carefully designing data models for the visual scene, we show that the emergence of this pattern is triggered by the non-Gaussian, higher-order local structure of the inputs, which has long been recognised as the hallmark of natural images. We provide an analytical and numerical characterisation of the pattern-formation mechanism responsible for this phenomenon in a simple model and find an unexpected link between receptive field formation and tensor decomposition of higher-order input correlations. These results provide a new perspective on the development of low-level feature detectors in various sensory modalities, and pave the way for studying the impact of higher-order statistics on learning in neural networks.

papers.title: Vision Transformer Visualization: What Neurons Tell and How Neurons Behave?
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers (ViTs) behave and what are their intriguing properties, such as robustness to image occlusions and patch shuffling?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a visualization technique to expose the information carried in neurons and embeddings across ViT layers, revealing that ViTs are robust to occlusions and patch shuffling, and that embeddings exhibit clustering behavior by object type at higher layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a visualization technique for ViTs, leading to findings including the clustering behavior of embeddings, which is explained mathematically and verified experimentally.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs are robust to image occlusions and patch shuffling, as visualized by the proposed technique.
Level 0 embeddings already carry rich semantic details, unlike CNNs where low-level filters capture only edges or lines.
Filters at layer 0 are powerful and can activate multiple object types across images.
Feature embeddings across layers show clustering behavior, becoming more separated by object type at higher layers, with higher attention weights for object patches.
A mathematical explanation is provided for the clustering behavior, and it is quantitatively verified on the Pascal VOC dataset.
papers.limitation: The clustering behavior of feature embeddings has not been exploited in real-world applications.
future_direction: Exploit the clustering behavior using contrastive learning to create more contrastive feature embeddings for downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Recently vision transformers (ViT) have been applied successfully for various tasks in computer vision. However, important questions such as why they work or how they behave still remain largely unknown. In this paper, we propose an effective visualization technique, to assist us in exposing the information carried in neurons and feature embeddings across the ViT's layers. Our approach departs from the computational process of ViTs with a focus on visualizing the local and global information in input images and the latent feature embeddings at multiple levels. Visualizations at the input and embeddings at level 0 reveal interesting findings such as providing support as to why ViTs are rather generally robust to image occlusions and patch shuffling; or unlike CNNs, level 0 embeddings already carry rich semantic details. Next, we develop a rigorous framework to perform effective visualizations across layers, exposing the effects of ViTs filters and grouping/clustering behaviors to object patches. Finally, we provide comprehensive experiments on real datasets to qualitatively and quantitatively demonstrate the merit of our proposed methods as well as our findings. https://github.com/byM1902/ViT_visualization

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: A Spectral Theory of Neural Prediction and Alignment
papers.research_question: Why do many different deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, and how can we differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a spectral theory that decomposes neural prediction error into model eigenspectra and alignment with neural data, and provides geometric measures (error mode radius Rem and dimension Dem) to interpret the error, revealing that different models can achieve similar prediction error through different geometric properties.
papers.conclusion: The spectral theory provides a framework to interpret neural prediction error and shows that geometric measures can differentiate models with similar prediction error, guiding future experiments and model design for improved neural activity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral theory accurately predicts neural prediction error for ridge regression from model activations to neural responses.
Error mode geometry (Rem and Dem) varies across models even when they have similar neural prediction error, providing additional insight into how models achieve low error.
Early model stages predict early visual areas (V1/V2) better, while later stages predict downstream areas (V4/IT) better, aligning with the hierarchical organization of the visual cortex.
Trained models have better alignment (Wi) with neural data than randomly initialized models, which is the main driver of improved prediction error.
Adversarial training improves alignment between model eigenvectors and early visual cortex activity, leading to lower prediction error in early areas.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical predictions are only accurate in the large P limit (large number of stimuli), and the tail eigenvalues of the empirical Gram matrix are often underestimated.
The results depend on the stimulus set used, which affects the model eigenspectra and thus the error mode geometry.
future_direction: Future work could consider choosing stimulus sets to maximize the difference between model eigenspectra, leading to greater differences in neural predictions.
Extending the theory to other regression methods and non-linear mappings between model activations and neural responses.
Applying the geometric measures to other domains beyond visual cortex to understand model representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: The representations of neural networks are often compared to those of biological systems by performing regression between the neural network responses and those measured from biological systems. Many different state-of-the-art deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, but it remains unclear how to differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses. To gain insight into this, we use a recent theoretical framework that relates the generalization error from regression to the spectral properties of the model and the target. We apply this theory to the case of regression between model activations and neural responses and decompose the neural prediction error in terms of the model eigenspectra, alignment of model eigenvectors and neural responses, and the training set size. Using this decomposition, we introduce geometrical measures to interpret the neural prediction error. We test a large number of deep neural networks that predict visual cortical activity and show that there are multiple types of geometries that result in low neural prediction error as measured via regression. The work demonstrates that carefully decomposing representational metrics can provide interpretability of how models are capturing neural activity and points the way towards improved models of neural activity.

papers.title: The Lazy Neuron Phenomenon: On Emergence of Activation Sparsity in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the prevalence, causes, and benefits of activation sparsity in Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that activation sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon in Transformers, arising from training dynamics, and that enforcing sparsity via Top-k Transformers improves efficiency, robustness, and calibration.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation sparsity is a fundamental property of trained Transformers with benefits for efficiency and reliability, and it may stem from training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Activation sparsity is prevalent in Transformers for both NLP and vision tasks, across all layers.
Larger Transformers (deeper and wider) are sparser in terms of percentage of nonzero activations.
Sparsity emerges even with random labels, random images, or infinite data, suggesting it is due to training dynamics rather than dataset properties.
Sparsity reduces FLOPs and can improve computational efficiency during inference.
Enforcing sparser activation via Top-k Transformers improves robustness to noisy training data, input corruptions, and calibration of prediction confidence.
papers.limitation: The benefit of sparse activation is not fully realized due to lack of hardware support for sparse computation.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the curious phenomenon for machine learning models with Transformer architectures that their activation maps are sparse. By activation map we refer to the intermediate output of the multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) after a ReLU activation function, and by sparse we mean that on average very few entries (e.g., 3.0% for T5-Base and 6.3% for ViT-B16) are nonzero for each input to MLP. Moreover, larger Transformers with more layers and wider MLP hidden dimensions are sparser as measured by the percentage of nonzero entries. Through extensive experiments we demonstrate that the emergence of sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon that occurs for both natural language processing and vision tasks, on both training and evaluation data, for Transformers of various configurations, at layers of all depth levels, as well as for other architectures including MLP-mixers and 2-layer MLPs. We show that sparsity also emerges using training datasets with random labels, or with random inputs, or with infinite amount of data, demonstrating that sparsity is not a result of a specific family of datasets. We discuss how sparsity immediately implies a way to significantly reduce the FLOP count and improve efficiency for Transformers. Moreover, we demonstrate perhaps surprisingly that enforcing an even sparser activation via Top-k thresholding with a small value of k brings a collection of desired but missing properties for Transformers, namely less sensitivity to noisy training data, more robustness to input corruptions, and better calibration for their prediction confidence.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Fine-Tuned Vision Transformers on Distorted Images: Decoding Attention Head Behavior for Transparent and Trustworthy AI
papers.research_question: How do individual attention heads in vision transformers process relevant versus extraneous information when fine-tuned on distorted images containing non-relevant content?
papers.core_contribution: This study uses attention map extraction and ablation analysis to show functional specialization in fine-tuned Vision Transformers, identifying monosemantic heads that focus on task-relevant features (chirp localization) and non-task-relevant features (text, edges), as well as polysemantic heads that attend to multiple irrelevant regions.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability, through attention map analysis and ablation, reveals functional specialization in Vision Transformers, enhancing model understanding and identifying components critical for task performance versus those processing irrelevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating attention heads in early layers (1-3) results in minimal performance impact, suggesting they focus on less critical low-level features.
Ablating deeper heads (e.g., in layer 6) causes a threefold higher loss increase, indicating greater importance for the regression task.
Intermediate layers (6-11) contain monosemantic heads that attend exclusively to the chirp region in spectrograms.
Some early heads (1-4) are monosemantic but non-task-relevant, specializing in detecting features like text, color bars, and edges/corners.
Attention maps can distinguish monosemantic heads (precise localization) from polysemantic heads (attending to multiple irrelevant regions).
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability improves the safety, reliability, and robustness of large AI models. This study examined individual attention heads in vision transformers (ViTs) fine tuned on distorted 2D spectrogram images containing non relevant content (axis labels, titles, color bars). By introducing extraneous features, the study analyzed how transformer components processed unrelated information, using mechanistic interpretability to debug issues and reveal insights into transformer architectures. Attention maps assessed head contributions across layers. Heads in early layers (1 to 3) showed minimal task impact with ablation increased MSE loss slightly ({\mu}=0.11%, {\sigma}=0.09%), indicating focus on less critical low level features. In contrast, deeper heads (e.g., layer 6) caused a threefold higher loss increase ({\mu}=0.34%, {\sigma}=0.02%), demonstrating greater task importance. Intermediate layers (6 to 11) exhibited monosemantic behavior, attending exclusively to chirp regions. Some early heads (1 to 4) were monosemantic but non task relevant (e.g. text detectors, edge or corner detectors). Attention maps distinguished monosemantic heads (precise chirp localization) from polysemantic heads (multiple irrelevant regions). These findings revealed functional specialization in ViTs, showing how heads processed relevant vs. extraneous information. By decomposing transformers into interpretable components, this work enhanced model understanding, identified vulnerabilities, and advanced safer, more transparent AI.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer-based Vision Models through Inversion
papers.research_question: How can feature inversion be used to interpret the internal representations of transformer-based vision models, and what insights does it provide about their processing of color, structure, and spatial information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a modular feature inversion method that is more efficient and scalable than the classic approach, and applies it to analyze DETR and ViT, revealing differences in their processing of color, structure, and spatial information.
papers.conclusion: Modular feature inversion is an efficient and effective tool for interpreting transformer-based vision models, revealing both shared properties (like gradual refinement) and distinct strategies (in color processing, structural abstraction, and spatial encoding) between DETR and ViT.
papers.key_findings:
DETR progressively abstracts object colors and shapes towards prototypical representations, while ViT preserves fine-grained visual details throughout its layers.
DETR is robust to color perturbations, whereas ViT's classification performance degrades under such changes.
ViT encodes spatial information in a localized manner, while DETR diffuses it more globally.
Both DETR and ViT exhibit gradual refinement of representations across their layers, a shared characteristic of transformer-based vision models.
The modular inversion approach, despite higher reconstruction error than the classic method, yields reconstructions better suited for network interpretability.
papers.limitation: It remains challenging to conclusively attribute specific properties in reconstructed images to individual processing stages without additional quantitative analysis.
future_direction: Explore how training data and objectives influence feature inversion results, e.g., by retraining architectures on the same dataset or swapping objectives.
Apply the modular inversion method to other modern vision models like DINOv2, SAM, or CNN-based architectures.
Investigate the use of feature inversion for error detection by comparing reconstructed images to inputs to identify discrepancies indicative of model failures.
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms underlying deep neural networks remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning and computer vision. One promising, yet only preliminarily explored approach, is feature inversion, which attempts to reconstruct images from intermediate representations using trained inverse neural networks. In this study, we revisit feature inversion, introducing a novel, modular variation that enables significantly more efficient application of the technique. We demonstrate how our method can be systematically applied to the large-scale transformer-based vision models, Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, and how reconstructed images can be qualitatively interpreted in a meaningful way. We further quantitatively evaluate our method, thereby uncovering underlying mechanisms of representing image features that emerge in the two transformer architectures. Our analysis reveals key insights into how these models encode contextual shape and image details, how their layers correlate, and their robustness against color perturbations. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of transformer-based vision models and their internal representations. The code for reproducing our experiments is available at github.com/wiskott-lab/inverse-tvm.

papers.title: Aligning Artificial Neural Networks and Ontologies towards Explainable AI
papers.research_question: Whether it is possible to relate the activations of a neural network with human-defined concepts from an ontology to generate symbolic justifications for the output of that neural network.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to generate human-comprehensible justifications for a neural network's output by mapping its internal activations to concepts from an ontology using small classifiers called mapping networks.
papers.conclusion: It is possible to leverage the knowledge hidden in a neural network's architecture to map its activations to ontological concepts and generate symbolic, human-comprehensible justifications for its output, increasing interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Mapping networks can extract human-defined ontological concepts from a neural network's activations if the concepts are relevant to the network's task.
Mapping networks require less training data and achieve higher accuracy than training a separate convolutional neural network to predict the same concepts from raw images.
An occlusion procedure shows that mapping networks correctly localize the visual features corresponding to the concepts they are trained to identify.
A feature selection procedure (Input Reduce) can significantly reduce the number of input features (activations) required for mapping networks while maintaining accuracy.
Using the extracted concepts and the ontology, symbolic justifications for the neural network's output can be generated, with correct justifications found in most test cases.
papers.limitation: The justifications obtained are not necessarily a representation of how neural networks really reach their outputs, but rather plausible and understandable justifications for how they might have achieved their results.
future_direction: Explore in-depth the extraction of justifications based on the ontology and the results of the mapping networks.
Investigate the usage of this method to search for learned biases in trained neural networks.
Use the method as a way to search for errors, missing axioms, or missing relations in ontologies.
papers.abstract: Neural networks have been the key to solve a variety of different problems. However, neural network models are still regarded as black boxes, since they do not provide any human-interpretable evidence as to why they output a certain result. We address this issue by leveraging on ontologies and building small classifiers that map a neural network model's internal state to concepts from an ontology, enabling the generation of symbolic justifications for the output of neural network models. Using an image classification problem as testing ground, we discuss how to map the internal state of a neural network to the concepts of an ontology, examine whether the results obtained by the established mappings match our understanding of the mapped concepts, and analyze the justifications obtained through this method.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of\n Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple types of features (facets) each neuron responds to, and improves activation maximization visualizations with more natural colors and coherent structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization by producing higher quality images and shows the multiple feature facets each neuron detects, providing a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level ones.
Multifaceted feature visualization produces more realistic and interpretable visualizations than previous activation maximization methods.
The method reveals that DNNs learn not only discriminative features but also global structure and context, similar to generative models.
Hidden fully connected layer neurons sometimes represent amalgams of different concepts.
papers.limitation:
The number of facets visualized depends on the manually set parameter k in k-means; automatically determining the true number of facets remains an open problem.
The method does not always reconstruct a proper facet (e.g., for stuffed peppers), possibly because the neuron ignores certain features.
Center-biased regularization is not guaranteed to produce a single object; it only biases optimization toward the center.
future_direction: Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron.
Investigating the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves visualization quality.
Further research into understanding the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons.
papers.abstract:
We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features
each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have
created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which
synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each
neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron
detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted,
in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example,
a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a
storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images
without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating
inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc.
Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of
each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of
images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that
produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images
obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of
image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate
colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus
provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each
neuron.

papers.title: Geometrization of deep networks for the interpretability of deep learning systems
papers.research_question: How can we understand deep learning systems? The paper proposes that geometrization of deep networks may provide a framework for interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a geometrization framework for deep networks, drawing analogies with image registration and physics, to provide a new perspective for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that geometrization provides a promising framework for interpreting deep learning systems, drawing connections to physics and geometry.
papers.key_findings:
Deep networks can be viewed as curves in a transformation space, and optimal networks correspond to geodesics.
The Fisher-Rao metric can be used to measure network complexity and generalization.
Batch normalization can be understood as encouraging the network to be geodesic-like.
The coupling of network structure and data is analogous to the coupling of spacetime and matter in general relativity.
The framework suggests that the ultimate interpretability may lie in a 'grand unified theory' of deep networks.
papers.limitation: The geometrization framework may not properly handle non-optimal deep networks, which are common in practice.
future_direction: Is there a GUT (grand unified theory) of deep networks?
How to geometrize reinforcement learning systems?
What’s the curvature of the emergent Fisher-Rao metric in deep networks?
papers.abstract: How to understand deep learning systems remains an open problem. In this paper we propose that the answer may lie in the geometrization of deep networks. Geometrization is a bridge to connect physics, geometry, deep network and quantum computation and this may result in a new scheme to reveal the rule of the physical world. By comparing the geometry of image matching and deep networks, we show that geometrization of deep networks can be used to understand existing deep learning systems and it may also help to solve the interpretability problem of deep learning systems.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.

papers.title: Vision Transformers Exhibit Human-Like Biases: Evidence of Orientation and Color Selectivity, Categorical Perception, and Phase Transitions
papers.research_question: This study explored whether Vision Transformers (ViTs) developed orientation and color biases similar to those observed in the human brain.
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers exhibit human-like perceptual biases, including an 'oblique effect' for horizontal orientations, categorical color perception, and phase transitions during training, which arise from pre-training and architectural constraints.
papers.conclusion: The observations suggest that biases and properties arise primarily from pre-training on the original dataset—which shapes the model's foundational representations—and the inherent architectural constraints of the vision transformer, rather than being solely determined by downstream data statistics.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs exhibited an 'oblique effect' showing the lowest angle prediction errors at 180° (horizontal) across all conditions.
Angle prediction errors varied by color, with highest errors for bluish hues and lowest for yellowish ones, and clustering analysis showed ViTs grouped colors in a way that aligned with human perceptual categories.
Training loss curves exhibited phase transitions (bumps), with delayed transitions when color was incorporated as an additional data attribute.
Attention heads in certain layers (e.g., heads 4, 5, and 12 in layer II) developed edge-detection specialization regardless of the downstream task, functioning as task-agnostic feature extractors.
Adding color increased noise sensitivity, degrading angle prediction performance under higher noise levels.
papers.limitation:
The use of simple line stimuli may not fully capture perceptual biases in real-world scenarios, where complex geometries and noise distributions could interact differently with visual processing.
The specific ViT circuits underlying orientation and color biases remain unclear.
The ViT was trained on a regression task (angle prediction), leaving open whether biases generalize to classification or generative tasks.
The interaction between color and orientation biases was not rigorously explained.
future_direction: Future work could address this by testing vision transformers (ViTs) on naturalistic datasets.
A mechanistic dissection of these circuits —such as how early layers resemble V1 edge detectors versus deeper, more categorical representations—would deepen our understanding.
Future studies could explore how these biases propagate across layers and tasks.
papers.abstract: This study explored whether Vision Transformers (ViTs) developed orientation and color biases similar to those observed in the human brain. Using synthetic datasets with controlled variations in noise levels, angles, lengths, widths, and colors, we analyzed the behavior of ViTs fine-tuned with LoRA. Our findings revealed four key insights: First, ViTs exhibited an oblique effect showing the lowest angle prediction errors at 180 deg (horizontal) across all conditions. Second, angle prediction errors varied by color. Errors were highest for bluish hues and lowest for yellowish ones. Additionally, clustering analysis of angle prediction errors showed that ViTs grouped colors in a way that aligned with human perceptual categories. In addition to orientation and color biases, we observed phase transition phenomena. While two phase transitions occurred consistently across all conditions, the training loss curves exhibited delayed transitions when color was incorporated as an additional data attribute. Finally, we observed that attention heads in certain layers inherently develop specialized capabilities, functioning as task-agnostic feature extractors regardless of the downstream task. These observations suggest that biases and properties arise primarily from pre-training on the original dataset which shapes the model's foundational representations and the inherent architectural constraints of the vision transformer, rather than being solely determined by downstream data statistics.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Explanatory Strategy for XAI
papers.research_question: How can the mechanistic explanatory strategy from philosophy of science be applied to explainable AI (XAI) for deep learning systems?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mechanistic explanatory strategy for XAI, drawing on neomechanistic philosophy, and illustrates its application to deep learning systems through case studies in image recognition and language modeling.
papers.conclusion: The mechanistic explanatory strategy for XAI, which focuses on identifying mechanisms in deep neural networks, offers significant epistemic benefits but faces challenges such as complexity and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic explanations can uncover elements that traditional explainability techniques might miss.
The mechanistic approach offers epistemic benefits such as enhanced interpretability, structural transparency, and the ability to craft counterfactual and generalizable explanations.
The approach aids in prediction and system manipulation by understanding internal dynamics.
The approach faces limitations including ambiguous effects on transparency, limited comprehensibility, the need for technical proficiency, and difficulties in decomposing complex systems.
Mechanistic decomposition can focus on functional analysis without covering every aspect of computational phenomena in concrete processing systems.
papers.limitation:
Ambiguous effects on algorithmic and run transparency.
Limited comprehensibility of explanations due to the lack of suitable concepts.
Necessity for recipients to have technical proficiency in AI.
Difficulties in decomposing complex, real-world systems, which are not evident in simpler toy model examples.
future_direction: Assess the applicability and scalability of the mechanistic approach beyond deep learning toy models to more complex AI systems.
Investigate how individual stakeholders comprehend mechanistic AI explanations through user studies complemented by a suitable epistemological theory of understanding.
Explore other philosophically informed explanatory strategies that thrive on system complexity and address other contexts of opacity.
papers.abstract: Despite significant advancements in XAI, scholars continue to note a persistent lack of robust conceptual foundations and integration with broader discourse on scientific explanation. In response, emerging XAI research increasingly draws on explanatory strategies from various scientific disciplines and the philosophy of science to address these gaps. This paper outlines a mechanistic strategy for explaining the functional organization of deep learning systems, situating recent developments in AI explainability within a broader philosophical context. According to the mechanistic approach, explaining opaque AI systems involves identifying the mechanisms underlying decision-making processes. For deep neural networks, this means discerning functionally relevant components - such as neurons, layers, circuits, or activation patterns - and understanding their roles through decomposition, localization, and recomposition. Proof-of-principle case studies from image recognition and language modeling align this theoretical framework with recent research from OpenAI and Anthropic. The findings suggest that pursuing mechanistic explanations can uncover elements that traditional explainability techniques may overlook, ultimately contributing to more thoroughly explainable AI.

papers.title: Interpretable Deep Learning: Interpretation, Interpretability, Trustworthiness, and Beyond
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of interpretation tools for deep neural networks, clarifying the concepts of interpretations and interpretability, and proposing a novel taxonomy for interpretation algorithms.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by summarizing the current state of interpretable deep learning and suggesting future research directions, including the need for more rigorous evaluation methods and the integration of interpretations into model training.
papers.key_findings:
The paper clarifies the distinction between interpretations (explanations generated by algorithms) and model interpretability (an intrinsic property of the model).
It proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy for interpretation algorithms based on representation, model type, and relation between algorithm and model.
It reviews various interpretation algorithms, including model-agnostic, gradient-based, and others.
It discusses evaluation methods for the trustworthiness of interpretation algorithms and model interpretability.
It connects interpretability with adversarial robustness and learning from interpretations.
future_direction: Exploring the connections between interpretation related terms and other properties of deep models.
Developing more model interpretability evaluation methods.
Integrating interpretations into training strategies to improve both interpretability and performance.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have been well-known for their superb handling of various machine learning and artificial intelligence tasks. However, due to their over-parameterized black-box nature, it is often difficult to understand the prediction results of deep models. In recent years, many interpretation tools have been proposed to explain or reveal how deep models make decisions. In this paper, we review this line of research and try to make a comprehensive survey. Specifically, we first introduce and clarify two basic concepts -- interpretations and interpretability -- that people usually get confused about. To address the research efforts in interpretations, we elaborate the designs of a number of interpretation algorithms, from different perspectives, by proposing a new taxonomy. Then, to understand the interpretation results, we also survey the performance metrics for evaluating interpretation algorithms. Further, we summarize the current works in evaluating models' interpretability using "trustworthy" interpretation algorithms. Finally, we review and discuss the connections between deep models' interpretations and other factors, such as adversarial robustness and learning from interpretations, and we introduce several open-source libraries for interpretation algorithms and evaluation approaches.

papers.title: An Introduction to Deep Visual Explanation
papers.research_question: How can we understand and explain the classification decisions of deep convolutional neural networks, especially when they produce unexpected results?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework called Deep Visual Explanation (DVE) that uses Fourier domain analysis of feature map activations to identify and visualize the discriminative pixels in an image that influence a DCNN's classification decision.
papers.conclusion: The DVE framework provides a way to explain DCNN decisions by capturing discriminative pixels through analysis of high and low spatial scale activations in the Fourier domain, demonstrated on image classification and a medical application.
papers.key_findings:
The DVE method can highlight discriminative image regions for both correct and incorrect network predictions.
A variant called targeted-DVE provides more precise explanations by penalizing less influential activations.
The method is computationally efficient and does not require retraining or architectural changes to the model.
Experiments show the network's predictions are sensitive to image blurring, indicating reliance on specific pixel-level features.
The method can be applied to sensitive domains like medical image classification to visualize the regions supporting a diagnosis.
papers.limitation: The framework is preliminary and has only been tested on image classification tasks; its extension to other domains like language or speech is future work.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other domains such as language and speech.
Develop more complex and interpretable explanations within the framework.
papers.abstract: The practical impact of deep learning on complex supervised learning problems has been significant, so much so that almost every Artificial Intelligence problem, or at least a portion thereof, has been somehow recast as a deep learning problem. The applications appeal is significant, but this appeal is increasingly challenged by what some call the challenge of explainability, or more generally the more traditional challenge of debuggability: if the outcomes of a deep learning process produce unexpected results (e.g., less than expected performance of a classifier), then there is little available in the way of theories or tools to help investigate the potential causes of such unexpected behavior, especially when this behavior could impact people's lives. We describe a preliminary framework to help address this issue, which we call "deep visual explanation" (DVE). "Deep," because it is the development and performance of deep neural network models that we want to understand. "Visual," because we believe that the most rapid insight into a complex multi-dimensional model is provided by appropriate visualization techniques, and "Explanation," because in the spectrum from instrumentation by inserting print statements to the abductive inference of explanatory hypotheses, we believe that the key to understanding deep learning relies on the identification and exposure of hypotheses about the performance behavior of a learned deep model. In the exposition of our preliminary framework, we use relatively straightforward image classification examples and a variety of choices on initial configuration of a deep model building scenario. By careful but not complicated instrumentation, we expose classification outcomes of deep models using visualization, and also show initial results for one potential application of interpretability.

papers.title: Emergent Semantics Beyond Token Embeddings: Transformer LMs with Frozen Visual Unicode Representations
papers.research_question: Can semantic understanding in Transformer language models emerge without trainable, semantically-rich input embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs with frozen, non-semantic visual Unicode embeddings can learn semantic understanding and outperform identical models with trainable embeddings on reasoning benchmarks, indicating semantics are an emergent property of the architecture, not the input embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Semantics in neural language models is not a property of the embedding matrix but an emergent phenomenon of the model's layered composition and self-attention, opening new avenues for model standardization, modularity, and efficient scaling.
papers.key_findings:
Models with frozen visual Unicode embeddings converge, generate coherent text, and outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark.
Semantic clustering emerges in the deeper transformer layers, not in the input embeddings, as shown by t-SNE visualizations.
Even randomly initialized frozen embeddings allow the model to converge, suggesting semantic structures in trainable embeddings are an emergent artifact, not a prerequisite.
The 'representational interference' hypothesis posits that trainable embeddings are burdened with learning both structural and semantic features, leading to suboptimal performance.
Frozen embeddings provide a stable structural foundation, freeing the transformer's attention and feed-forward layers to focus on composing these primitives into high-level meaning.
papers.limitation:
The study was intentionally constrained in scale (0.3B parameters, 4B tokens); future work should test whether findings hold for models at the 10B+ parameter scale.
Generalization to truly novel modalities (e.g., mathematical formulas, chemical structures) remains an open question.
future_direction: Test whether these findings hold for models at the 10B+ parameter scale.
Explore the method's generalization to novel modalities (e.g., mathematical formulas, chemical structures).
Investigate applications in modular and standardized embeddings, efficient Mixture-of-Experts, and cross-lingual transfer.
papers.abstract: Understanding the locus of semantic representation in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for interpretability and architectural innovation. The dominant paradigm posits that trainable input embeddings serve as foundational "meaning vectors." This paper challenges that view. We construct Transformer models where the embedding layer is entirely frozen, with vectors derived not from data, but from the visual structure of Unicode glyphs. These non-semantic, precomputed visual embeddings are fixed throughout training. Our method is compatible with any tokenizer, including a novel Unicode-centric tokenizer we introduce to ensure universal text coverage. Despite the absence of trainable, semantically initialized embeddings, our models converge, generate coherent text, and, critically, outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark. We attribute this to "representational interference" in conventional models, where the embedding layer is burdened with learning both structural and semantic features. Our results indicate that high-level semantics are not inherent to input embeddings but are an emergent property of the Transformer's compositional architecture and data scale. This reframes the role of embeddings from meaning containers to structural primitives. We release all code and models to foster further research.

papers.title: Aligning Machine and Human Visual Representations across Abstraction Levels
papers.research_question: What is missing for modern learning systems to exhibit more human-aligned behavior? The paper investigates the misalignment between vision models and humans in capturing hierarchical conceptual knowledge and proposes a method to address it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces AligNet, a method to align vision model representations with human hierarchical conceptual knowledge by distilling human-aligned similarity structures, resulting in models that are more human-aligned and generalize better.
papers.conclusion: Aligning model representations with human judgments yields more robust, interpretable, and human-aligned AI systems, demonstrating a path towards better artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
AligNet fine-tuning significantly improves alignment with human similarity judgments across multiple levels of abstraction.
Aligned models show better generalization in few-shot learning and out-of-distribution robustness.
Model representations reorganize according to semantic hierarchy after alignment.
Alignment benefits various vision foundation models regardless of their pretraining objectives.
Human response times correlate better with model uncertainties after alignment.
papers.limitation:
models we used neither account for context in similarity judgments nor higher-order relations.
human representations may vary systematically across individuals, cultures, and so on.
human judgment is full of flaws, intrinsic contradictions and discrepancies.
future_direction: explore how to best learn from human knowledge without adopting human imperfections.
applying alignment techniques to other areas like natural language processing.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved success across a wide range of applications, including as models of human behavior and neural representations in vision tasks. However, neural network training and human learning differ in fundamental ways, and neural networks often fail to generalize as robustly as humans do raising questions regarding the similarity of their underlying representations. What is missing for modern learning systems to exhibit more human-aligned behavior? We highlight a key misalignment between vision models and humans: whereas human conceptual knowledge is hierarchically organized from fine- to coarse-scale distinctions, model representations do not accurately capture all these levels of abstraction. To address this misalignment, we first train a teacher model to imitate human judgments, then transfer human-aligned structure from its representations to refine the representations of pretrained state-of-the-art vision foundation models via finetuning. These human-aligned models more accurately approximate human behavior and uncertainty across a wide range of similarity tasks, including a new dataset of human judgments spanning multiple levels of semantic abstractions. They also perform better on a diverse set of machine learning tasks, increasing generalization and out-of-distribution robustness. Thus, infusing neural networks with additional human knowledge yields a best-of-both-worlds representation that is both more consistent with human cognitive judgments and more practically useful, thus paving the way toward more robust, interpretable, and human-aligned artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Learning Features and their Transformations by Spatial and Temporal\n Spherical Clustering
papers.research_question: How can a neural model learn features invariant to arbitrary transformations in spatiotemporal data, inspired by simple and complex cells in the primary visual cortex?
papers.core_contribution: A novel two-layered feedforward neural model that learns transformation-invariant features via spatial spherical clustering in the first layer and temporal spherical clustering in the second layer, enabling online unsupervised learning, topographic map formation, and prediction.
papers.conclusion: The proposed model is an ideal candidate to be used as a canonical computational unit in hierarchical networks for real-world applications and for understanding biological brain functions.
papers.key_findings:
First layer neurons develop simple cell-like receptive fields (small unoriented features, Gabor-like filters, edge-detectors) when exposed to natural videos.
Second layer neurons develop complex cell-like response properties, learning transformations and showing invariance.
The model learns a topographic map of spatial features by exploiting temporal continuity and physical constraints, minimizing wiring length.
The model can make higher-order predictions by combining learned transformations in the complex layer with transition probabilities from lateral connections in the simple layer.
The system's entropy converges during learning from natural stimuli.
papers.abstract:
Learning features invariant to arbitrary transformations in the data is a
requirement for any recognition system, biological or artificial. It is now
widely accepted that simple cells in the primary visual cortex respond to
features while the complex cells respond to features invariant to different
transformations. We present a novel two-layered feedforward neural model that
learns features in the first layer by spatial spherical clustering and
invariance to transformations in the second layer by temporal spherical
clustering. Learning occurs in an online and unsupervised manner following the
Hebbian rule. When exposed to natural videos acquired by a camera mounted on a
cat's head, the first and second layer neurons in our model develop simple and
complex cell-like receptive field properties. The model can predict by learning
lateral connections among the first layer neurons. A topographic map to their
spatial features emerges by exponentially decaying the flow of activation with
distance from one neuron to another in the first layer that fire in close
temporal proximity, thereby minimizing the pooling length in an online manner
simultaneously with feature learning.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail.
