Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Vision Transformers Need Registers
papers.research_question: Why do artifacts (high-norm tokens) appear in feature maps of vision transformers, and how can they be fixed?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies artifacts (high-norm tokens) in vision transformer feature maps and proposes a simple fix by adding register tokens to the input sequence, which removes artifacts and improves performance on dense prediction tasks and object discovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper exposes artifacts in vision transformer feature maps, proposes adding register tokens as a simple fix, and demonstrates its effectiveness across supervised, text-supervised, and self-supervised models.
papers.key_findings:
Artifacts correspond to high-norm tokens that appear primarily in low-informative background areas of images.
These high-norm tokens hold global image information but little local patch information.
Adding register tokens to the input sequence entirely removes the artifacts, leading to smoother feature and attention maps.
Models trained with register tokens show improved performance on dense prediction tasks like segmentation and depth estimation.
Register tokens enable object discovery methods (e.g., LOST) to work effectively with modern vision transformers.
papers.limitation: The authors have not been able to fully determine which aspects of the training led to the appearance of artifacts in different models.
future_direction: Study the regularization of registers.
Investigate why the value projection in OpenCLIP filters out outliers even without registers.
papers.abstract: Transformers have recently emerged as a powerful tool for learning visual representations. In this paper, we identify and characterize artifacts in feature maps of both supervised and self-supervised ViT networks. The artifacts correspond to high-norm tokens appearing during inference primarily in low-informative background areas of images, that are repurposed for internal computations. We propose a simple yet effective solution based on providing additional tokens to the input sequence of the Vision Transformer to fill that role. We show that this solution fixes that problem entirely for both supervised and self-supervised models, sets a new state of the art for self-supervised visual models on dense visual prediction tasks, enables object discovery methods with larger models, and most importantly leads to smoother feature maps and attention maps for downstream visual processing.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Improving Neuron-level Interpretability with White-box Language Models
papers.research_question: Can building sparsity directly into the language model architecture (via a white-box design) improve neuron-level interpretability compared to post-hoc methods like sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a white-box transformer-like architecture (crate) that embeds sparse coding directly into the model, leading to significantly improved neuron-level interpretability compared to standard transformers like GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: Replacing the standard transformer architecture with the white-box crate model significantly improves neuron-level interpretability, pointing towards a promising direction for building more interpretable foundation models with built-in sparse coding.
papers.key_findings:
crate achieves up to 103% relative improvement in neuron-level interpretability over GPT-2 across multiple evaluation metrics.
The improved interpretability is steady across different layers and model sizes.
crate's interpretability stems from its ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens.
crate has more optimal representations for interpretability than GPT-2, as applying sparse autoencoders (SAE) to crate yields smaller improvements than applying SAE to GPT-2.
crate can be steered without the reconstruction loss inherent in post-hoc SAE methods.
papers.limitation: The performance of crate on the next-token prediction task is not as good as GPT-2, potentially due to the introduction of sparsity.
future_direction: Investigate a better trade-off between performance and interpretability in language models with built-in sparsity.
Research more qualitative mechanisms in white-box language models and how to use them for downstream edits.
papers.abstract: Neurons in auto-regressive language models like GPT-2 can be interpreted by analyzing their activation patterns. Recent studies have shown that techniques such as dictionary learning, a form of post-hoc sparse coding, enhance this neuron-level interpretability. In our research, we are driven by the goal to fundamentally improve neural network interpretability by embedding sparse coding directly within the model architecture, rather than applying it as an afterthought. In our study, we introduce a white-box transformer-like architecture named Coding RAte TransformEr (CRATE), explicitly engineered to capture sparse, low-dimensional structures within data distributions. Our comprehensive experiments showcase significant improvements (up to 103% relative improvement) in neuron-level interpretability across a variety of evaluation metrics. Detailed investigations confirm that this enhanced interpretability is steady across different layers irrespective of the model size, underlining CRATE's robust performance in enhancing neural network interpretability. Further analysis shows that CRATE's increased interpretability comes from its enhanced ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens. These findings point towards a promising direction for creating white-box foundation models that excel in neuron-level interpretation.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: How Learnable Grids Recover Fine Detail in Low Dimensions: A Neural Tangent Kernel Analysis of Multigrid Parametric Encodings
papers.research_question: Why do multigrid parametric encodings (MPEs) often outperform Fourier feature encodings (FFEs) in learning high-frequency details in low-dimensional mappings, and how does the structure of MPEs affect the neural tangent kernel (NTK) spectrum?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that multigrid parametric encodings (MPEs) improve a network's ability to learn high-frequency details by raising the eigenvalue spectrum of the neural tangent kernel (NTK), and that this improvement stems from the learnable grid structure rather than just the embedding space, unlike Fourier feature encodings (FFEs).
papers.conclusion: MPEs mitigate spectral bias in a fundamentally different way than FFEs by leveraging learnable grid parameters to raise the NTK eigenvalue spectrum, enabling better learning of high-frequency details in low-dimensional mappings.
papers.key_findings:
MPEs increase the minimum eigenvalue of the NTK by 8 orders of magnitude over the baseline MLP and 2 orders of magnitude over the FFE, corresponding to significant gains in PSNR and MS-SSIM.
The performance improvement of MPEs is isolated to their learnable grid parameters, not the embedding space, which is fundamentally different from FFEs that rely solely on the embedding.
The eigenvalue spectrum of the NTK is a reliable predictor of a network's ability to learn high-frequency details, with higher spectra leading to better performance.
MPEs outperform FFEs in learning fine details in both 2D image regression and 3D implicit surface regression tasks.
The NTK spectrum remains relatively stable during the latter half of training, validating its use for analysis.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not account for the influence of different activation functions.
The space of possible problems is too large to compute the NTK for each application.
future_direction: Optimizing encodings for specific applications by adjusting the interpolation kernel or tuning hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Neural networks that map between low dimensional spaces are ubiquitous in computer graphics and scientific computing; however, in their naive implementation, they are unable to learn high frequency information. We present a comprehensive analysis comparing the two most common techniques for mitigating this spectral bias: Fourier feature encodings (FFE) and multigrid parametric encodings (MPE). FFEs are seen as the standard for low dimensional mappings, but MPEs often outperform them and learn representations with higher resolution and finer detail. FFE's roots in the Fourier transform, make it susceptible to aliasing if pushed too far, while MPEs, which use a learned grid structure, have no such limitation. To understand the difference in performance, we use the neural tangent kernel (NTK) to evaluate these encodings through the lens of an analogous kernel regression. By finding a lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue of the NTK, we prove that MPEs improve a network's performance through the structure of their grid and not their learnable embedding. This mechanism is fundamentally different from FFEs, which rely solely on their embedding space to improve performance. Results are empirically validated on a 2D image regression task using images taken from 100 synonym sets of ImageNet and 3D implicit surface regression on objects from the Stanford graphics dataset. Using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and multiscale structural similarity (MS-SSIM) to evaluate how well fine details are learned, we show that the MPE increases the minimum eigenvalue by 8 orders of magnitude over the baseline and 2 orders of magnitude over the FFE. The increase in spectrum corresponds to a 15 dB (PSNR) / 0.65 (MS-SSIM) increase over baseline and a 12 dB (PSNR) / 0.33 (MS-SSIM) increase over the FFE.

papers.title: Sequential Interpretability: Methods, Applications, and Future Direction for Understanding Deep Learning Models in the Context of Sequential Data
papers.research_question: What are the current techniques for interpreting deep learning models that process sequential data, and what are the limitations and future directions for this research area?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review and taxonomy of interpretability techniques specifically for deep learning models that process sequential data, categorizing methods into network analysis, sequential saliency, and multivariate attribution, and identifies gaps and future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper summarizes the current state of interpretability techniques for deep sequential models, presents a goal-oriented taxonomy, and highlights specific limitations and opportunities for future research in data modalities, application domains, and interpretable techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The majority of interpretability research has focused on image processing, with less attention on sequential data despite its importance in domains like NLP and healthcare.
Interpretability techniques for sequential data can be categorized into three primary trends: network analysis (e.g., weight inspection, maximum activation), sequential saliency (e.g., attention, gradient-based saliency), and multivariate attribution (e.g., dual attention mechanisms, backwards neuron attribution).
Attention mechanisms have become a widespread form of sequential interpretability but have drawbacks, such as being easily manipulated and not always reliably indicating the most predictive input features.
There is a notable lack of interpretable frameworks for video data and for modeling sequences as arbitrary-length subsequences rather than contiguous single time steps.
Several domain- and model-agnostic interpretability approaches (e.g., LIME, meta-learning, adversarial techniques) have not yet been explored or demonstrated for sequential data and applications.
papers.limitation:
The most common data type in the reviewed literature is text, followed by time series, discrete sequences, and video, with a surprising lack of interpretable frameworks for video processing.
Nearly all reviewed works identify salient subsequences as contiguous, single salient time steps rather than by directly modeling a sequence as a series of arbitrary length subsequences.
Several domain- and model-agnostic interpretability approaches (e.g., LIME, meta learning, deep nearest neighbors, adversarial techniques) have not been explored or demonstrated for sequential data.
future_direction: Extending interpretability research to video data modalities.
Developing methods to model sequences as series of arbitrary-length subsequences rather than just contiguous time steps.
Exploring and demonstrating general interpretability methods (like LIME, meta-learning, adversarial techniques) for sequential data and applications.
papers.abstract: Deep learning continues to revolutionize an ever-growing number of critical application areas including healthcare, transportation, finance, and basic sciences. Despite their increased predictive power, model transparency and human explainability remain a significant challenge due to the "black box" nature of modern deep learning models. In many cases the desired balance between interpretability and performance is predominately task specific. Human-centric domains such as healthcare necessitate a renewed focus on understanding how and why these frameworks are arriving at critical and potentially life-or-death decisions. Given the quantity of research and empirical successes of deep learning for computer vision, most of the existing interpretability research has focused on image processing techniques. Comparatively, less attention has been paid to interpreting deep learning frameworks using sequential data. Given recent deep learning advancements in highly sequential domains such as natural language processing and physiological signal processing, the need for deep sequential explanations is at an all-time high. In this paper, we review current techniques for interpreting deep learning techniques involving sequential data, identify similarities to non-sequential methods, and discuss current limitations and future avenues of sequential interpretability research.

papers.title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining
papers.research_question: When exactly do induction heads emerge in language models, and what properties of natural language give rise to induction heads formation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the emergence point of induction heads, which is agnostic to model size; that bigram repetition frequency and reliability affect IH formation with a Pareto frontier; and that local dependency with high frequency and reliability is sufficient for IH formation, but when these are low, categoriality and marginal distribution shape matter.
papers.conclusion: The emergence of induction heads can be predicted by batch size and context size; frequency and reliability of bigram repetitions define a Pareto frontier for IH formation; and local dependency with high frequency and reliability always leads to IH formation, while categoriality matters only near the frontier.
papers.key_findings:
A simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the point at which induction heads form, and this emergence point is agnostic to model size.
Surface bigram repetition frequency and reliability strongly affect the formation of induction heads, and there is an effective Pareto frontier in terms of these two values.
Local dependency with high bigram repetition frequency and reliability is sufficient for induction head formation, but when the frequency and reliability are low, categoriality and the shape of the marginal distribution matter.
papers.limitation: Due to limited compute resources, only models up to 350M parameters were trained and up to 7B parameters used for inference, so it is unclear if trends hold for larger models.
future_direction: Extend the study to larger models and other behavioral phases in language model pretraining.
Study the effect of other data properties, such as long-range dependencies, on induction head formation.
Investigate whether the predictive law generalizes to other behavioral phases.
papers.abstract: Specialized attention heads dubbed induction heads (IHs) have been argued to underlie the remarkable in-context learning capabilities of modern language models; yet, a precise characterization of their emergence, especially in the context of language modeling, remains wanting. In this study, we investigate the relationship between statistical properties of the training data and IH formation in both natural and synthetic training data settings. We show that: (1) A simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the point at which IHs form and that this emergence point is agnostic to model size; (2) Surface bigram repetition frequency and reliability strongly affect the formation of IHs, and we find an effective Pareto frontier in terms of these two values; (3) local dependency with high bigram repetition frequency and reliability is sufficient for IH formation, but when the frequency and reliability are low, categoriality and the shape of the marginal distribution matter.

papers.title: The Inductive Bottleneck: Data-Driven Emergence of Representational Sparsity in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Is the inductive bottleneck (U-shaped entropy profile) in Vision Transformers an inherent property of the Self-Attention mechanism, or a dynamic reaction to the statistical properties of the training data?
papers.core_contribution: The inductive bottleneck (U-shaped entropy profile) in Vision Transformers is not an architectural artifact but a data-dependent adaptation that correlates with the semantic abstraction required by the task.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bottleneck is a data-driven emergence of representational sparsity in Vision Transformers, demonstrating that ViTs are dynamic hierarchy networks that build their own bottlenecks on demand.
papers.key_findings:
The depth of the bottleneck correlates strongly with the semantic abstraction required by the task.
For texture-heavy datasets (UC Merced), the network maintains high-rank representations throughout all layers.
For object-centric datasets (CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet), the network compresses information in middle layers to isolate semantic features.
The bottleneck is an active compression mechanism learned by the network.
Vanilla ViTs can emulate hierarchical compression like Swin Transformers but in a flexible, data-dependent manner.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to ViT-Small; it is unclear if larger models exhibit the same relative percentages.
The study focused on Classification/DINO; it is unclear if Dense Prediction tasks (Segmentation, Detection) would prevent bottleneck formation.
No causal intervention (e.g., forcing low rank) was performed to test if the bottleneck improves performance.
future_direction: Explore if ViT-Large or ViT-Huge exhibit the same relative percentages or add more 'Phantom Dimensions'.
Investigate if Dense Prediction tasks (Segmentation, Detection) prevent bottleneck formation.
Perform causal intervention (e.g., forcing low rank) to see if it improves performance, and explore 'Spectral Pruning' during training.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) lack the hierarchical inductive biases inherent to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), theoretically allowing them to maintain high-dimensional representations throughout all layers. However, recent observations suggest ViTs often spontaneously manifest a "U-shaped" entropy profile-compressing information in middle layers before expanding it for the final classification. In this work, we demonstrate that this "Inductive Bottleneck" is not an architectural artifact, but a data-dependent adaptation. By analyzing the layer-wise Effective Encoding Dimension (EED) of DINO-trained ViTs across datasets of varying compositional complexity (UC Merced, Tiny ImageNet, and CIFAR-100), we show that the depth of the bottleneck correlates strongly with the semantic abstraction required by the task. We find that while texture-heavy datasets preserve high-rank representations throughout, object-centric datasets drive the network to dampen high-frequency information in middle layers, effectively "learning" a bottleneck to isolate semantic features.

papers.title: The geometry of BERT
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention mechanism work internally, and what insights can be gained about its classification process?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel theoretical perspective on BERT's attention mechanism, introducing the concepts of directionality of subspace selection and cone index, and analyzes attention patterns and global information flow to understand its classification process.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
The attention mechanism in BERT performs a subspace selection driven by the searching engine process (Q, K, V matrices).
The self-attention matrix exhibits specific, classifiable patterns (e.g., directional gate, open gate, contextual gates) that convey different types of information.
The cone index and distribution analysis show that lower layers specialize in finding information content, while upper layers primarily propagate it.
The information content propagates globally as a mean information content; the MLP synthesizes information from different heads, breaking the channel structure.
Rank collapse in attention is reinterpreted as a potential carrier of directional information rather than a purely negative phenomenon.
future_direction: Analysis of the BERT learning process during training.
Examining the specialization of individual components in the BERT architecture.
Leveraging these findings to optimize the architecture of the Transformer encoder.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks, particularly Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), have shown remarkable performance across various tasks such as classification, text summarization, and question answering. However, their internal mechanisms remain mathematically obscure, highlighting the need for greater explainability and interpretability. In this direction, this paper investigates the internal mechanisms of BERT proposing a novel perspective on the attention mechanism of BERT from a theoretical perspective. The analysis encompasses both local and global network behavior. At the local level, the concept of directionality of subspace selection as well as a comprehensive study of the patterns emerging from the self-attention matrix are presented. Additionally, this work explores the semantic content of the information stream through data distribution analysis and global statistical measures including the novel concept of cone index. A case study on the classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants using RNA which resulted in a very high accuracy has been selected in order to observe these concepts in an application. The insights gained from this analysis contribute to a deeper understanding of BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models and further analysis in the training process.

papers.title: How Transformers Get Rich: Approximation and Dynamics Analysis
papers.research_question: How do transformers implement induction heads, both in terms of approximation and learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis showing how two-layer transformers can approximate induction heads and characterizes the training dynamics with a sharp transition from n-gram to induction head learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently implement induction heads through specific roles of submodules, and learning induction heads involves a sharp transition from n-gram mechanisms driven by time-scale separation and component proportions.
papers.key_findings:
Two-layer single-head transformers without FFNs can approximate vanilla induction heads.
Two-layer multi-head transformers without FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads (in-context n-gram).
Two-layer multi-head transformers with FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads with generic similarity functions.
Training dynamics on a mixed target show a sharp transition from 4-gram to induction head, with four phases.
The transition is driven by time-scale separation in self-attention and speed differences due to component proportions.
papers.limitation:
Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding may be nontrivial.
Dynamics analysis is limited to a simple mixed target without FFNs.
future_direction: Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding.
Generalizing dynamics analysis to nonlinear functions with FFNs.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated exceptional in-context learning capabilities, yet the theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanisms remains limited. A recent work (Elhage et al., 2021) identified a ``rich'' in-context mechanism known as induction head, contrasting with ``lazy'' $n$-gram models that overlook long-range dependencies. In this work, we provide both approximation and dynamics analyses of how transformers implement induction heads. In the {\em approximation} analysis, we formalize both standard and generalized induction head mechanisms, and examine how transformers can efficiently implement them, with an emphasis on the distinct role of each transformer submodule. For the {\em dynamics} analysis, we study the training dynamics on a synthetic mixed target, composed of a 4-gram and an in-context 2-gram component. This controlled setting allows us to precisely characterize the entire training process and uncover an {\em abrupt transition} from lazy (4-gram) to rich (induction head) mechanisms as training progresses.

papers.title: Deep Networks as Logical Circuits: Generalization and Interpretation
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how deep neural networks generalize despite having high capacity, and proposes a method to interpret them as logical circuits.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to exactly represent a deep neural network as a logical circuit of linear classifiers, providing both interpretability and generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The logical circuit formulation is a powerful method for analyzing, interpreting, and improving DNNs, connecting interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs trained on linearly separable data learn linear classifiers regardless of architecture depth.
The logical circuit representation can be much simpler than the original network, requiring fewer parameters.
The method can interpret DNNs on MNIST, revealing that intermediate logical computations correspond to semantically meaningful digit categories.
Generalization can be improved by diagnosing and replacing memorizing components in the logical circuit.
Theoretical generalization bounds based on the logical circuit are favorable compared to norm-based bounds and are robust to increasing depth.
papers.limitation: The efficient determination of network states (¯Σ0) analytically from weights is an open problem, limiting application to high-dimensional datasets.
future_direction: Extending the logical circuit approach to other datasets.
Developing efficient algorithms to determine network states analytically.
papers.abstract: Not only are Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) black box models, but also we frequently conceptualize them as such. We lack good interpretations of the mechanisms linking inputs to outputs. Therefore, we find it difficult to analyze in human-meaningful terms (1) what the network learned and (2) whether the network learned. We present a hierarchical decomposition of the DNN discrete classification map into logical (AND/OR) combinations of intermediate (True/False) classifiers of the input. Those classifiers that can not be further decomposed, called atoms, are (interpretable) linear classifiers. Taken together, we obtain a logical circuit with linear classifier inputs that computes the same label as the DNN. This circuit does not structurally resemble the network architecture, and it may require many fewer parameters, depending on the configuration of weights. In these cases, we obtain simultaneously an interpretation and generalization bound (for the original DNN), connecting two fronts which have historically been investigated separately. Unlike compression techniques, our representation is. We motivate the utility of this perspective by studying DNNs in simple, controlled settings, where we obtain superior generalization bounds despite using only combinatorial information (e.g. no margin information). We demonstrate how to "open the black box" on the MNIST dataset. We show that the learned, internal, logical computations correspond to semantically meaningful (unlabeled) categories that allow DNN descriptions in plain English. We improve the generalization of an already trained network by interpreting, diagnosing, and replacing components the logical circuit that is the DNN.

papers.title: Learning Sparse Visual Representations via Spatial-Semantic Factorization
papers.research_question: How can we resolve the conflict between semantic understanding and image reconstruction in self-supervised visual representation learning by factorizing features into sparse semantic tokens and spatial distributions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STELLAR, a framework that factorizes visual features into a low-rank product of sparse semantic tokens and their spatial distributions, enabling simultaneous high-quality image reconstruction and rich semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The trade-off between semantic abstraction and spatial grounding is an artifact of dense-grid representations, and STELLAR resolves this by factorizing the latent space into sparse 'what' and 'where' components.
papers.key_findings:
STELLAR achieves a state-of-the-art balance of semantics (79.10% ImageNet accuracy) and reconstruction (FID 2.60) with as few as 16 tokens.
The factorized representation enables equivariant partitioning: semantic tokens remain invariant to spatial transformations while localization matrices change equivariantly.
STELLAR outperforms reconstruction-based and joint-embedding baselines on fine-grained understanding tasks like semantic segmentation.
Ablation studies show that low-rank reconstruction, concept clustering, and set alignment are all critical components.
STELLAR can be trained from random initialization or from foundational priors (MAE, DINO) and consistently improves semantic and spatial grounding.
papers.limitation: STELLAR underperforms on global classification for simple object-centric datasets because averaging token features can dilute discriminative information.
future_direction: Integrating STELLAR concepts with linguistic embeddings for more interpretable multimodal understanding with Large Language Models.
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) faces a fundamental conflict between semantic understanding and image reconstruction. High-level semantic SSL (e.g., DINO) relies on global tokens that are forced to be location-invariant for augmentation alignment, a process that inherently discards the spatial coordinates required for reconstruction. Conversely, generative SSL (e.g., MAE) preserves dense feature grids for reconstruction but fails to produce high-level abstractions. We introduce STELLAR, a framework that resolves this tension by factorizing visual features into a low-rank product of semantic concepts and their spatial distributions. This disentanglement allows us to perform DINO-style augmentation alignment on the semantic tokens while maintaining the precise spatial mapping in the localization matrix necessary for pixel-level reconstruction. We demonstrate that as few as 16 sparse tokens under this factorized form are sufficient to simultaneously support high-quality reconstruction (2.60 FID) and match the semantic performance of dense backbones (79.10% ImageNet accuracy). Our results highlight STELLAR as a versatile sparse representation that bridges the gap between discriminative and generative vision by strategically separating semantic identity from spatial geometry. Code available at https://aka.ms/stellar.

papers.title: SPARO: Selective Attention for Robust and Compositional Transformer Encodings for Vision
papers.research_question: Can adding a selective attention mechanism that partitions transformer encodings into separately-attended slots improve robustness and compositionality in representation learning models like CLIP and DINO?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparo, a read-out mechanism that partitions transformer encodings into separately-attended slots produced by single-head attention, improving robustness and compositionality in CLIP and DINO without increasing model size.
papers.conclusion: Sparo imparts a prior for compositionality and selective attention in transformer encodings, leading to improved generalization, robustness, and compositionality in representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Sparo improves zero-shot recognition, robustness, and compositionality for CLIP across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +14% on ImageNet, +4% on SugarCrepe).
Sparo improves linear probe and nearest neighbors performance for DINO (+3% each on ImageNet).
Post-hoc selection of Sparo slots based on task relevance further improves compositionality (e.g., from +4% to +9% on SugarCrepe).
Ablations show that separate-head attention and slot-wise operations are critical for Sparo's performance gains.
Visualizations show that Sparo slots attend to distinct concepts like subjects, activities, and locations.
papers.limitation:
Visualizing attended positions only shows where information is taken from, not how it is used.
No explicit independence or disentanglement constraints are imposed on the learned slots.
future_direction: Explore auxiliary training objectives to impose stronger distributional conditions on learned concepts.
Develop more sophisticated post-hoc concept selection methods, such as using human interaction or set cover algorithms.
papers.abstract: Selective attention helps us focus on task-relevant aspects in the constant flood of our sensory input. This constraint in our perception allows us to robustly generalize under distractions and to new compositions of perceivable concepts. Transformers employ a similar notion of attention in their architecture, but representation learning models with transformer backbones like CLIP and DINO often fail to demonstrate robustness and compositionality. We highlight a missing architectural prior: unlike human perception, transformer encodings do not separately attend over individual concepts. In response, we propose SPARO, a read-out mechanism that partitions encodings into separately-attended slots, each produced by a single attention head. Using SPARO with CLIP imparts an inductive bias that the vision and text modalities are different views of a shared compositional world with the same corresponding concepts. Using SPARO, we demonstrate improvements on downstream recognition, robustness, retrieval, and compositionality benchmarks with CLIP (up to +14% for ImageNet, +4% for SugarCrepe), and on nearest neighbors and linear probe for ImageNet with DINO (+3% each). We also showcase a powerful ability to intervene and select individual SPARO concepts to further improve downstream task performance (up from +4% to +9% for SugarCrepe) and use this ability to study the robustness of SPARO's representation structure. Finally, we provide insights through ablation experiments and visualization of learned concepts.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Clarifying Model Transparency: Interpretability versus Explainability in Deep Learning with MNIST and IMDB Examples
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between interpretability (global understanding of model mechanisms) and explainability (local explanations for individual predictions) in deep learning, as demonstrated through MNIST and IMDB case studies?
papers.core_contribution: Clarifies the distinction between interpretability (global understanding of model internal operations) and explainability (post-hoc local explanations) in deep learning, using MNIST and IMDB examples to show that local explainability can be achieved even when global interpretability is limited.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is associated with inherent comprehensibility of model internal operations for global understanding, while explainability involves post-hoc methods for local explanations. Progress requires advancements in both intrinsically interpretable models and robust explainability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability focuses on global understanding of model internals, while explainability provides local explanations for specific predictions.
Post-hoc XAI methods like SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM can generate local explanations for opaque models such as CNNs and Transformers.
Local explanations do not confer global interpretability; a model can be explainable without being interpretable.
There is a trade-off between model performance and transparency, where high-accuracy models often lack global interpretability.
Both interpretability and explainability are vital for building trust, debugging, ensuring fairness, and meeting regulatory compliance in AI systems.
papers.limitation:
Performance vs. Transparency Trade-off: High-accuracy DL models frequently lack global interpretability, and simpler interpretable models might compromise predictive power.
Veracity of Explanations: Validating that local explanations genuinely mirror the model's reasoning for a specific instance remains a significant hurdle.
Human-Centricity of Explanations: The definition of an effective or 'understandable' local explanation is inherently subjective and varies with context and user.
Objective Evaluation: Quantifying the quality of global interpretability or a local explanation poses considerable difficulty.
Resource Intensiveness: Many XAI techniques demand substantial computational resources.
future_direction: Development of Inherently Interpretable Deep Learning Systems
Advancement of Causal Explanations
Creation of Interactive and Personalized Explanation Interfaces
papers.abstract: The impressive capabilities of deep learning models are often counterbalanced by their inherent opacity, commonly termed the "black box" problem, which impedes their widespread acceptance in high-trust domains. In response, the intersecting disciplines of interpretability and explainability, collectively falling under the Explainable AI (XAI) umbrella, have become focal points of research. Although these terms are frequently used as synonyms, they carry distinct conceptual weights. This document offers a comparative exploration of interpretability and explainability within the deep learning paradigm, carefully outlining their respective definitions, objectives, prevalent methodologies, and inherent difficulties. Through illustrative examinations of the MNIST digit classification task and IMDB sentiment analysis, we substantiate a key argument: interpretability generally pertains to a model's inherent capacity for human comprehension of its operational mechanisms (global understanding), whereas explainability is more commonly associated with post-hoc techniques designed to illuminate the basis for a model's individual predictions or behaviors (local explanations). For example, feature attribution methods can reveal why a specific MNIST image is recognized as a '7', and word-level importance can clarify an IMDB sentiment outcome. However, these local insights do not render the complex underlying model globally transparent. A clear grasp of this differentiation, as demonstrated by these standard datasets, is vital for fostering dependable and sound artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: One-layer transformers fail to solve the induction heads task
papers.research_question: What are the size limitations of one-layer transformers in solving the induction heads task compared to two-layer transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that one-layer transformers cannot solve the induction heads task unless they are exponentially larger than two-layer transformers, using a communication complexity argument.
papers.conclusion: One-layer transformers are fundamentally limited in solving the induction heads task efficiently compared to two-layer transformers.
papers.key_findings: One-layer transformers require size hmp = Ω(n) to solve the induction heads task, which is exponentially larger than the size sufficient for two-layer transformers.
papers.abstract: A simple communication complexity argument proves that no one-layer transformer can solve the induction heads task unless its size is exponentially larger than the size sufficient for a two-layer transformer.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
papers.research_question: Do commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones?
papers.core_contribution: Common SAE metrics (e.g., auto-interpretability scores) do not reliably distinguish between trained and randomly initialized transformers, indicating these metrics are insufficient for validating interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: High aggregate auto-interpretability scores alone do not guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered; the paper recommends routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics similar to those from trained models.
Standard SAE quality metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm) show similar trends across trained and randomized variants.
Token distribution entropy reveals that features from randomized models remain simple and token-specific, unlike features from trained models which become more abstract across layers.
The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for auto-interpretability tasks does not meaningfully discriminate between trained and randomized transformers in many settings.
Randomly initialized neural networks can preserve or amplify superposition present in input data, which may explain the similar SAE performance.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia models and the RedPajama dataset; results may vary with other architectures or data.
future_direction: Develop better metrics to distinguish between artifacts and genuinely learned computations in interpretability methods.
Investigate why randomly initialized transformers produce SAE metrics similar to trained ones, e.g., whether they preserve or amplify superposition.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.

papers.title: A Multimodal Automated Interpretability Agent
papers.research_question: How can we build tools that combine the flexibility of human experimentation with the scalability of automated techniques for neural model understanding, specifically for tasks like feature interpretation and failure mode discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MAIA, a multimodal agent that automates interpretability tasks by composing tools for iterative experimentation, and demonstrates its ability to describe neurons and aid in tasks like spurious feature removal and bias identification.
papers.conclusion: MAIA is a step towards automating interpretability, but fully automating end-to-end interpretation of other systems will require more advanced tools and agents with more advanced reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
MAIA produces neuron descriptions comparable to those generated by expert human experimenters.
MAIA can identify and help reduce sensitivity to spurious features in a classifier.
MAIA can automatically identify inputs likely to be mis-classified and reveal biases in neuron behavior.
MAIA's performance improves with better tools, such as using DALL-E 3 for image generation.
MAIA's modular design allows for flexible evaluation of arbitrary systems and incorporation of new tools.
papers.limitation:
MAIA can exhibit confirmation bias and may draw conclusions from small sample sizes.
Image generation and editing tools (e.g., Stable Diffusion, InstructPix2Pix) sometimes fail to faithfully generate or edit images according to instructions, which can confuse MAIA.
future_direction: Fully automating end-to-end interpretation will require more advanced tools and agents with more advanced reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: This paper describes MAIA, a Multimodal Automated Interpretability Agent. MAIA is a system that uses neural models to automate neural model understanding tasks like feature interpretation and failure mode discovery. It equips a pre-trained vision-language model with a set of tools that support iterative experimentation on subcomponents of other models to explain their behavior. These include tools commonly used by human interpretability researchers: for synthesizing and editing inputs, computing maximally activating exemplars from real-world datasets, and summarizing and describing experimental results. Interpretability experiments proposed by MAIA compose these tools to describe and explain system behavior. We evaluate applications of MAIA to computer vision models. We first characterize MAIA's ability to describe (neuron-level) features in learned representations of images. Across several trained models and a novel dataset of synthetic vision neurons with paired ground-truth descriptions, MAIA produces descriptions comparable to those generated by expert human experimenters. We then show that MAIA can aid in two additional interpretability tasks: reducing sensitivity to spurious features, and automatically identifying inputs likely to be mis-classified.

papers.title: Using Degeneracy in the Loss Landscape for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does degeneracy in neural network parameterizations obfuscate internal structure for mechanistic interpretability, and how can we remove these degeneracies to obtain more interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of degeneracy in neural network parameterizations as an obstacle to interpretability, characterizes three sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis, a technique to obtain a representation invariant to these degeneracies, which may lead to sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that degeneracy in neural network parameterizations hinders interpretability, identifies sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis to remove degeneracies, potentially yielding sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters can be degenerate due to linear dependence between activations in a layer, linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer, and ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints.
Modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and a metric for identifying modules is developed based on this argument.
The Interaction Basis is a tractable technique to obtain a representation invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.
Representations invariant to degeneracies are likely to have sparser interactions.
The effective parameter count, derived from the local learning coefficient, measures the number of computationally relevant parameters in the network.
papers.limitation: The derivation of the Interaction Basis relies on two simplifying assumptions of independence about the Hessian, which are strong assumptions.
future_direction: Investigate alternative techniques for finding a basis without the simplifying assumptions about the Hessian.
Determine how to choose an appropriate behavioral loss cutoff epsilon for finite data singular learning theory.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to reverse engineer the algorithms implemented by neural networks by studying their weights and activations. An obstacle to reverse engineering neural networks is that many of the parameters inside a network are not involved in the computation being implemented by the network. These degenerate parameters may obfuscate internal structure. Singular learning theory teaches us that neural network parameterizations are biased towards being more degenerate, and parameterizations with more degeneracy are likely to generalize further. We identify 3 ways that network parameters can be degenerate: linear dependence between activations in a layer; linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer; ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints. We also present a heuristic argument that modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and we develop a metric for identifying modules in a network that is based on this argument. We propose that if we can represent a neural network in a way that is invariant to reparameterizations that exploit the degeneracies, then this representation is likely to be more interpretable, and we provide some evidence that such a representation is likely to have sparser interactions. We introduce the Interaction Basis, a tractable technique to obtain a representation that is invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.

papers.title: CLASSIFICATION OF STELLAR SPECTRA WITH LOCAL LINEAR EMBEDDING
papers.abstract: We investigate the use of dimensionality reduction techniques for the classification of stellar spectra selected from the SDSS. Using local linear embedding (LLE), a technique that preserves the local (and possibly non-linear) structure within high dimensional data sets, we show that the majority of stellar spectra can be represented as a one dimensional sequence within a three dimensional space. The position along this sequence is highly correlated with spectral temperature. Deviations from this "stellar locus" are indicative of spectra with strong emission lines (including misclassified galaxies) or broad absorption lines (e.g. Carbon stars). Based on this analysis, we propose a hierarchical classification scheme using LLE that progressively identifies and classifies stellar spectra in a manner that requires no feature extraction and that can reproduce the classic MK classifications to an accuracy of one type.

papers.title: Examining vision foundation models for classification and detection in optical and radio astronomy
papers.abstract: Context . Vision foundation models, which have demonstrated significant potential in many multimedia applications, are often underutilized in the natural sciences. This is primarily due to mismatches between the nature of domain-specific scientific data and the typical training data used for foundation models, leading to distribution shifts. Scientific data often differ substantially in structure and characteristics, and researchers frequently face the challenge of optimizing model performance with limited labeled data of only a few hundred or thousand images. Aims . This work evaluates the performance of vision foundation models in astrophysics, with a focus on identifying the best practices for adapting these models to domain-specific datasets. We aim to establish a framework for selecting, fine-tuning, and optimizing these models for common tasks in optical and radio astronomy. Methods .
