papers.conclusion: BIMT is an innovative and practical approach to neural network interpretability, enabling more efficient and effective circuit discovery, which is critical for analyzing large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
BIMT achieves lower logit difference (1.2737 for circle detection) compared to other training regimes, indicating better circuit quality.
BIMT discovers circuits faster (93.76 seconds for circle detection) than other models.
BIMT produces sparser circuits (0.9859 sparsity for circle detection) which are easier to interpret.
BIMT requires more memory during training due to the swap operation, and has longer training times.
BIMT has slightly higher inference times compared to L1-only model (65.77 vs 64.65 seconds for 500000 images).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the MNIST dataset and MLP architecture, which may not generalize to other tasks and models.
Modular training may cause neurons to become polysemantic due to superposition, which could hinder interpretability.
future_direction: Test BIMT on transformer networks.
Investigate the effect of modularity on superposition.
Use attribution patching instead of activation patching for larger networks.
Evaluate BIMT on other tasks beyond digit classification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have experienced a rapid rise in AI, changing a wide range of applications with their advanced capabilities. As these models become increasingly integral to decision-making, the need for thorough interpretability has never been more critical. Mechanistic Interpretability offers a pathway to this understanding by identifying and analyzing specific sub-networks or 'circuits' within these complex systems. A crucial aspect of this approach is Automated Circuit Discovery, which facilitates the study of large models like GPT4 or LLAMA in a feasible manner. In this context, our research evaluates a recent method, Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), designed to enhance the interpretability of neural networks. We demonstrate how BIMT significantly improves the efficiency and quality of Automated Circuit Discovery, overcoming the limitations of manual methods. Our comparative analysis further reveals that BIMT outperforms existing models in terms of circuit quality, discovery time, and sparsity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive computational analysis of BIMT, including aspects such as training duration, memory allocation requirements, and inference speed. This study advances the larger objective of creating trustworthy and transparent AI systems in addition to demonstrating how well BIMT works to make neural networks easier to understand.

papers.title: Studying Cross-cluster Modularity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of training neural networks to be modular using a clusterability loss on interpretability, such as task specialization and circuit size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a clusterability measure and loss function to train neural networks to be modular. Shows that modular models do not exhibit more task specialization but have smaller circuits, aiding interpretability.
papers.conclusion: A simple regularizer can split neural network layers into non-interacting modules, but these modules do not yield expected interpretability benefits like task specialization. However, modularity improves circuit size and search space without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models are not modular; clusters are highly enmeshed.
Training with clusterability loss effectively increases modularity in models.
Modular models do not show increased task specialization compared to non-modular models.
Modular models have smaller effective circuits, reducing circuit size.
Theoretical analysis indicates modularity simplifies function spaces and reduces the number of features.
papers.limitation: The modularity metric does not lead to clear interpretability benefits such as task specialization.
future_direction: Investigate alternative regularizers for interpretability benefits.
Build an automated subtask detection mechanism.
papers.abstract: An approach to improve neural network interpretability is via clusterability, i.e., splitting a model into disjoint clusters that can be studied independently. We define a measure for clusterability and show that pre-trained models form highly enmeshed clusters via spectral graph clustering. We thus train models to be more modular using a "clusterability loss" function that encourages the formation of non-interacting clusters. We then investigate the emerging properties of these highly clustered models. We find our trained clustered models do not exhibit more task specialization, but do form smaller circuits. We investigate CNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR, small transformers trained on modular addition, and GPT-2 and Pythia on the Wiki dataset, and Gemma on a Chemistry dataset. This investigation shows what to expect from clustered models.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Toward Transparent AI: A Survey on Interpreting the Inner Structures of Deep Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: This survey reviews over 300 works on inner interpretability for deep neural networks, introduces a taxonomy classifying methods by what part of the network they explain and whether they are intrinsic or post hoc, and discusses challenges and future directions to make interpretability tools more useful for engineers.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability research should focus on producing tools that are useful to engineers, with an emphasis on diagnostics, debugging, adversaries, benchmarking, and leveraging combinations of different interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
The paper introduces a taxonomy for inner interpretability methods, categorizing them by the part of the network they explain (weights, neurons, subnetworks, or latent representations) and by when they are applied (intrinsic or post hoc).
It highlights connections between interpretability and other research areas such as adversarial robustness, continual learning, modularity, network compression, and the human visual system.
The survey argues that the current status quo in interpretability research is largely unproductive and calls for a shift towards engineering-focused work that emphasizes diagnostics, debugging, adversaries, and benchmarking.
papers.limitation: Rapid progress in the field has made a thorough systematization of methods difficult.
future_direction: More work on diagnostics, debugging, adversaries, and benchmarking to make interpretability tools more useful in practical applications.
Applying interpretability techniques for debugging and debiasing in real-world models.
Growing the field of interpretability and seeing it as a requirement for deployed systems.
A paradigm shift toward engineering, focusing on producing tools that are competitive in real applications.
papers.abstract: The last decade of machine learning has seen drastic increases in scale and capabilities. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly being deployed in the real world. However, they are difficult to analyze, raising concerns about using them without a rigorous understanding of how they function. Effective tools for interpreting them will be important for building more trustworthy AI by helping to identify problems, fix bugs, and improve basic understanding. In particular, "inner" interpretability techniques, which focus on explaining the internal components of DNNs, are well-suited for developing a mechanistic understanding, guiding manual modifications, and reverse engineering solutions. Much recent work has focused on DNN interpretability, and rapid progress has thus far made a thorough systematization of methods difficult. In this survey, we review over 300 works with a focus on inner interpretability tools. We introduce a taxonomy that classifies methods by what part of the network they help to explain (weights, neurons, subnetworks, or latent representations) and whether they are implemented during (intrinsic) or after (post hoc) training. To our knowledge, we are also the first to survey a number of connections between interpretability research and work in adversarial robustness, continual learning, modularity, network compression, and studying the human visual system. We discuss key challenges and argue that the status quo in interpretability research is largely unproductive. Finally, we highlight the importance of future work that emphasizes diagnostics, debugging, adversaries, and benchmarking in order to make interpretability tools more useful to engineers in practical applications.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Deep Supervised, but Not Unsupervised, Models May Explain IT Cortical Representation
papers.research_question: To what extent can the internal representations of computational object-vision models explain the representational geometry of primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex?
papers.core_contribution: Supervised deep learning models, particularly a deep convolutional network trained on ImageNet, best explain the representational geometry of primate IT cortex, and combining their features with linear discriminants can fully explain the IT data, whereas unsupervised models fail to account for the categorical clustering in IT.
papers.conclusion: Explaining IT cortical representation requires computational features trained through supervised learning with large labeled datasets to emphasize behaviorally important categorical divisions.
papers.key_findings:
Better performing models in object categorization show higher representational similarity to IT cortex.
Unsupervised models fail to explain the categorical clustering (e.g., animate/inanimate, face clusters) observed in IT.
A deep supervised convolutional network (trained on ImageNet) best explains IT representation but does not fully explain it.
Combining features from the deep supervised model with linear discriminants (trained to maximize categorical margins) yields a representation that fully explains the IT data.
Model representations that are more similar to IT also afford better categorization accuracy.
papers.abstract: Inferior temporal (IT) cortex in human and nonhuman primates serves visual object recognition. Computational object-vision models, although continually improving, do not yet reach human performance. It is unclear to what extent the internal representations of computational models can explain the IT representation. Here we investigate a wide range of computational model representations (37 in total), testing their categorization performance and their ability to account for the IT representational geometry. The models include well-known neuroscientific object-recognition models (e.g. HMAX, VisNet) along with several models from computer vision (e.g. SIFT, GIST, self-similarity features, and a deep convolutional neural network). We compared the representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) of the model representations with the RDMs obtained from human IT (measured with fMRI) and monkey IT (measured with cell recording) for the same set of stimuli (not used in training the models). Better performing models were more similar to IT in that they showed greater clustering of representational patterns by category. In addition, better performing models also more strongly resembled IT in terms of their within-category representational dissimilarities. Representational geometries were significantly correlated between IT and many of the models. However, the categorical clustering observed in IT was largely unexplained by the unsupervised models. The deep convolutional network, which was trained by supervision with over a million category-labeled images, reached the highest categorization performance and also best explained IT, although it did not fully explain the IT data. Combining the features of this model with appropriate weights and adding linear combinations that maximize the margin between animate and inanimate objects and between faces and other objects yielded a representation that fully explained our IT data. Overall, our results suggest that explaining IT requires computational features trained through supervised learning to emphasize the behaviorally important categorical divisions prominently reflected in IT.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Interpretability of deep-learning methods applied to large-scale structure surveys
papers.research_question: What parts and features of large-scale structure survey data are most important in a convolutional neural network's prediction process for cosmological parameter estimation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a data degradation approach to interpret CNN predictions in cosmology, finding that the network uses both Gaussian and non-Gaussian information, with key importance of scales at the linear/non-linear transition.
papers.conclusion: The convolutional neural network's constraining performance is strongest when provided with both Gaussian and non-Gaussian information, and structures at the limit between linear and non-linear regimes are particularly important in its prediction process.
papers.key_findings:
The scales 8-12 Mpc/h (transition between linear and non-linear regimes) are most informative for the CNN.
Mid convergence regions hold little information alone, but improve performance when combined with extreme (low or high) convergence regions.
Presenting data in Fourier space significantly degrades performance, indicating the CNN architecture is designed for real-space images.
Summing redshift bins (removing tomography) does not degrade performance in the baseline model without intrinsic alignment, but does when intrinsic alignment is included.
Removing all spatial information via pixel shuffling still allows some prediction, with performance similar to a power spectrum approach.
papers.limitation:
The approach requires re-training the network for each degradation, which is computationally expensive.
The baseline model does not include astrophysical uncertainties like intrinsic alignment, which affects some conclusions.
papers.abstract: Deep learning and convolutional neural networks in particular are powerful and promising tools for cosmological analysis of large-scale structure surveys. They are already providing similar performance to classical analysis methods using fixed summary statistics, are showing potential to break key degeneracies by better probe combination and will likely improve rapidly in the coming years as progress is made in the physical modelling through both software and hardware improvement. One key issue remains: unlike classical analysis, a convolutional neural network's decision process is hidden from the user as the network optimises millions of parameters with no direct physical meaning. This prevents a clear understanding of the potential limitations and biases of the analysis, making it hard to rely on as a main analysis method. In this work, we explore the behaviour of such a convolutional neural network through a novel method. Instead of trying to analyse a network a posteriori, i.e. after training has been completed, we study the impact on the constraining power of training the network and predicting parameters with degraded data where we removed part of the information. This allows us to gain an understanding of which parts and features of a large-scale structure survey are most important in the network's prediction process. We find that the network's prediction process relies on a mix of both Gaussian and non-Gaussian information, and seems to put an emphasis on structures whose scales are at the limit between linear and non-linear regimes.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Towards interpretable-by-design deep learning algorithms
papers.research_question: How can deep learning models be made interpretable by design using prototypes, and how does this approach perform in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and resistance to confounding without requiring finetuning of the backbone model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the IDEAL framework, which transforms standard deep learning models into interpretable, prototype-based models without necessarily requiring finetuning, achieving competitive performance, especially with Vision Transformer backbones, while offering inherent interpretability and robustness to confounding.
papers.conclusion: The IDEAL framework offers an interpretable-by-design alternative to standard deep learning that can match the performance of opaque models, especially when using modern architectures like ViT, without the need for computationally expensive finetuning, and is effective for lifelong learning and mitigating confounding biases.
papers.key_findings:
The IDEAL framework without finetuning achieves performance competitive with finetuned models, with the gap being especially small for Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures.
The framework provides interpretability through real-image prototypes, allowing users to see which training examples a prediction is based on.
IDEAL circumvents catastrophic forgetting and enables efficient class-incremental learning, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on benchmarks like iCIFAR-100.
Without finetuning, IDEAL improves performance on confounded data compared to finetuned counterparts by avoiding overfitting to spurious correlations.
The choice of prototype selection method (e.g., k-means) is crucial for performance when the backbone is not finetuned, but becomes less significant when the backbone is finetuned.
papers.abstract: The proposed framework named IDEAL (Interpretable-by-design DEep learning ALgorithms) recasts the standard supervised classification problem into a function of similarity to a set of prototypes derived from the training data, while taking advantage of existing latent spaces of large neural networks forming so-called Foundation Models (FM). This addresses the issue of explainability (stage B) while retaining the benefits from the tremendous achievements offered by DL models (e.g., visual transformers, ViT) pre-trained on huge data sets such as IG-3.6B + ImageNet-1K or LVD-142M (stage A). We show that one can turn such DL models into conceptually simpler, explainable-through-prototypes ones. The key findings can be summarized as follows: (1) the proposed models are interpretable through prototypes, mitigating the issue of confounded interpretations, (2) the proposed IDEAL framework circumvents the issue of catastrophic forgetting allowing efficient class-incremental learning, and (3) the proposed IDEAL approach demonstrates that ViT architectures narrow the gap between finetuned and non-finetuned models allowing for transfer learning in a fraction of time \textbf{without} finetuning of the feature space on a target dataset with iterative supervised methods.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: Interpreting vision transformers via residual replacement model
papers.research_question: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable SAE features in the residual stream, enabling scalable circuit discovery and application to debiasing spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: The residual replacement model provides a faithful and interpretable framework for understanding ViT mechanisms, with practical utility in tasks like debiasing.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features in ViTs are interpretable across all layers, evolving from low-level attributes to high-level semantic concepts.
ViTs encode specialized features such as curve detectors and position detectors, analogous to those in CNNs and LMs.
The residual replacement model produces parsimonious circuits that faithfully explain ViT mechanisms, with improvements from edge-based discovery and gradient correction.
The framework enables quantitative analysis of feature similarity across layers, showing convergence for intra-class images.
The model can be applied to debias spurious correlations in ImageNet classifiers through feature ablation.
future_direction: Incorporating higher-order interactions between intermediate features in the gradient-based decomposition.
papers.abstract: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world? This paper addresses this long-standing question through the first systematic analysis of 6.6K features across all layers, extracted via sparse autoencoders, and by introducing the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable features in the residual stream. Our analysis reveals not only a feature evolution from low-level patterns to high-level semantics, but also how ViTs encode curves and spatial positions through specialized feature types. The residual replacement model scalably produces a faithful yet parsimonious circuit for human-scale interpretability by significantly simplifying the original computations. As a result, this framework enables intuitive understanding of ViT mechanisms. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our framework in debiasing spurious correlations.

papers.title: The Representational Status of Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether deep learning models are representational in a relational sense and to what extent they are semantically decomposable.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that deep learning models are representational in a relational sense, but they are minimally semantically decomposable (holistic) models, and there is no evidence that they encode locally decomposable representations of their targets.
papers.conclusion: Deep learning models are best conceived as holistic representational models, and interpreting them as locally decomposable is epistemically risky.
papers.key_findings:
Deep learning models are representational in a relational sense (they have real targets).
Deep learning models are not locally semantically decomposable; their representational capacity is global/holistic.
Opacity blocks a full assessment of the representational status of deep learning models.
Attempts to interpret deep learning models as locally decomposable are underdetermined and unfalsifiable.
The degree of idealization of a deep learning model cannot be evaluated due to opacity.
future_direction: Future analysis on situating deep learning models in the wider class of holistic models.
Exploring how deep learning models can be leveraged for scientific discovery without relying on local decomposability.
papers.abstract: This paper aims to clarify the representational status of Deep Learning Models (DLMs). While commonly referred to as 'representations', what this entails is ambiguous due to a conflation of functional and relational conceptions of representation. This paper argues that while DLMs represent their targets in a relational sense, in general, we have no good reason to believe that DLMs encode locally semantically decomposable representations of their targets. That is, the representational capacity these models have is largely global, rather than decomposable into stable, local subrepresentations. This result has immediate implications for explainable AI (XAI) and directs attention toward exploring the global relational nature of deep learning representations and their relationship both to models more generally to understand their potential role in future scientific inquiry.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: PAHQ: Accelerating Automated Circuit Discovery through Mixed-Precision Inference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can automated circuit discovery be accelerated while maintaining faithfulness, addressing its computational inefficiency and high memory requirements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PAHQ, a training-free mixed-precision quantization method that accelerates automated circuit discovery by maintaining high precision for critical attention heads and reducing precision elsewhere, achieving significant speedup and memory reduction with minimal faithfulness loss.
papers.conclusion: PAHQ provides an efficient acceleration approach for mechanistic interpretability research without sacrificing analytical quality, making circuit discovery more computationally feasible.
papers.key_findings:
PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80% and memory consumption by up to 30% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness.
PAHQ outperforms RTN quantization and Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) in terms of AUC-ROC on circuit discovery tasks like IOI, Docstring, and Greater Than.
The method is training-free and readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism.
PAHQ's selective precision allocation and three-stream parallel scheduler effectively mask data transfer latency, enabling near-optimal throughput.
The method scales effectively to larger transformer models (GPT-2-medium, large, XL) while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
PAHQ is designed for algorithms that evaluate edges sequentially (like ACDC) and may not be as effective for methods that evaluate multiple edges simultaneously (like EAP).
