PAHQ makes circuit discovery more feasible for moderately larger models but does not solve the scalability challenge for foundation models with hundreds of billions of parameters.
The method is empirically validated but lacks theoretical analysis on how high-precision signals propagate through lower-precision layers.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery, which involves identifying sparse and task-relevant subnetworks in pre-trained language models, is a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. Automated Circuit Discovery (ACDC) has emerged as a pivotal methodology in circuit discovery, but its application to large language models is severely limited by computational inefficiency and prohibitively high memory requirements. Although several accelerated approaches have been proposed, they primarily rely on linear approximations to ACDC, which significantly compromises analytical faithfulness. Our proposed method for accelerating automated circuit discovery, Per Attention Head Quantization (PAHQ), takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing the efficiency of each individual patching operation. PAHQ leverages a fundamental alignment between activation patching and mixed-precision quantization (MPQ): interpretability analysis through patching essentially performs targeted ablation studies. Therefore, we can maintain high precision exclusively for investigated components while safely reducing precision elsewhere in the network. PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80\% and memory consumption by up to 30\% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness. Importantly, our method readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism. This training-free approach provides a practical and novel pathway for accelerating mechanistic interpretability methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/626619403/PAHQ.

papers.title: Amortized Spectral Kernel Discovery via Prior-Data Fitted Network
papers.research_question: How can we extract explicit spectral densities and stationary kernels from pre-trained Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) to improve interpretability and enable downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework and decoder architectures to extract explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels from the latent representations of frozen Prior-Data Fitted Networks, enabling amortized kernel discovery without iterative optimization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that PFNs implicitly encode structured spectral information, which can be decoded into explicit, portable kernel representations, bridging the gap between amortized inference and interpretable kernel discovery for scientific and downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic analysis shows the attention latent output (H) in PFNs encodes the spectral content of the input function, forming a smooth manifold correlated with frequency.
The proposed Filter Bank Decoder can recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and construct explicit stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem.
Decoded kernels achieve Gaussian process regression performance comparable to the original PFN and optimization-based baselines (Deep Kernel Learning, Random Fourier Features) while requiring only a single forward pass, yielding orders-of-magnitude inference speedups.
Theoretical analysis characterizes the identifiability limits of spectral density: spectral weights are non-identifiable from a single normalized realization but become identifiable with multiple independent realizations.
The framework operates effectively in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, with an analytical scaling module to resolve global scale ambiguity in the single-function setting.
papers.limitation:
The decoded kernels are explicit stationary surrogate kernels obtained via Bochner's theorem; they are not exact reconstructions of the PFN's internal attention mechanism nor guaranteed to match the true data-generating GP kernel.
In the single-realization setting, spectral weights are not identifiable from a single normalized function sample, limiting full spectral recovery.
papers.abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) enable efficient amortized inference but lack transparent access to their learned priors and kernels. This opacity hinders their use in downstream tasks, such as surrogate-based optimization, that require explicit covariance models. We introduce an interpretability-driven framework for amortized spectral discovery from pre-trained PFNs with decoupled attention. We perform a mechanistic analysis on a trained PFN that identifies attention latent output as the key intermediary, linking observed function data to spectral structure. Building on this insight, we propose decoder architectures that map PFN latents to explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem. We study this pipeline in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, contextualizing theoretical limits on spectral identifiability and proving consistency when multiple function samples are available. Empirically, the proposed decoders recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and produce explicit kernels that support Gaussian process regression with accuracy comparable to PFNs and optimization-based baselines, while requiring only a single forward pass. This yields orders-of-magnitude reductions in inference time compared to optimization-based baselines.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
future_direction: Extend concept definition to include a broader set of clinical metrics.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB Shared Task: Improving Circuit Faithfulness via Better Edge Selection
papers.research_question: How to improve circuit faithfulness via better edge selection in circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes bootstrapping, positive-negative ratio (PNR), and integer linear programming (ILP) for edge selection in circuit discovery, improving faithfulness over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Principled edge selection improves faithfulness and enables more robust circuit discovery, despite computational limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Bootstrapping identifies edges with consistent attribution scores, filtering out unstable ones.
Positive-negative ratio (PNR) selection balances positive and negative edges, improving circuit faithfulness.
Integer linear programming (ILP) provides globally optimal edge selection compared to greedy algorithms.
Combinations of these methods outperform baseline approaches across multiple models and tasks on MIB metrics.
papers.limitation:
ILP optimization scales poorly with edge count, limiting applicability to larger models.
Optimal ratio of positive edges varies by models and tasks, requiring task-specific tuning.
Gap between state-of-the-art attribution methods and 'ground truth' edge importance scores limits faithfulness gains from ILP.
papers.abstract: One of the main challenges in mechanistic interpretability is circuit discovery, determining which parts of a model perform a given task. We build on the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB) and propose three key improvements to circuit discovery. First, we use bootstrapping to identify edges with consistent attribution scores. Second, we introduce a simple ratio-based selection strategy to prioritize strong positive-scoring edges, balancing performance and faithfulness. Third, we replace the standard greedy selection with an integer linear programming formulation. Our methods yield more faithful circuits and outperform prior approaches across multiple MIB tasks and models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/MIB-Shared-Task.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Visual Interpretability for Deep Learning: a Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper reviews recent studies in understanding neural-network representations and learning neural networks with interpretable/disentangled middle-layer representations, with a focus on convolutional neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that visualization, disentanglement, and learning of interpretable representations are key directions, and middle-to-end learning based on interpretable representations is a promising future trend.
papers.key_findings:
Visualization of CNN representations is the most direct way to explore network representations and provides a technical foundation for many diagnostic approaches.
Disentangling CNN features into explanatory graphs or decision trees provides a more thorough explanation of network representations.
Learning neural networks with interpretable/disentangled representations presents significant challenges, with only a few studies published in this direction.
Evaluation metrics for network interpretability, such as filter interpretability and location instability, are crucial but challenging to define and develop.
Interpretable representations enable semantic-level middle-to-end learning, which can significantly reduce the requirement for human annotation and allow human-computer interaction.
future_direction: middle-to-end learning
debugging CNN representations at the semantic level
papers.abstract: This paper reviews recent studies in understanding neural-network representations and learning neural networks with interpretable/disentangled middle-layer representations. Although deep neural networks have exhibited superior performance in various tasks, the interpretability is always the Achilles' heel of deep neural networks. At present, deep neural networks obtain high discrimination power at the cost of low interpretability of their black-box representations. We believe that high model interpretability may help people to break several bottlenecks of deep learning, e.g., learning from very few annotations, learning via human-computer communications at the semantic level, and semantically debugging network representations. We focus on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and we revisit the visualization of CNN representations, methods of diagnosing representations of pre-trained CNNs, approaches for disentangling pre-trained CNN representations, learning of CNNs with disentangled representations, and middle-to-end learning based on model interpretability. Finally, we discuss prospective trends in explainable artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Into the Rabbit Hull: From Task-Relevant Concepts in DINO to Minkowski Geometry
papers.research_question: What is the nature of DINOv2's internal representations? Specifically, what concepts are encoded, how are they used in downstream tasks, and how are they geometrically organized?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a large-scale concept analysis of DINOv2 using sparse autoencoders, revealing functional specialization of concepts across downstream tasks, and proposes the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis (MRH) which posits that activations are organized as Minkowski sums of convex polytopes rather than as sparse linear directions.
papers.conclusion: DINOv2's representations are organized beyond pure linear sparsity, and the proposed Minkowski Representation Hypothesis offers a refined geometric view with implications for how we study, steer, and interpret vision-transformer representations.
papers.key_findings:
Different downstream tasks recruit distinct families of concepts: classification relies on 'Elsewhere' detectors that implement learned negation, segmentation on boundary concepts forming coherent subspaces, and depth estimation on three distinct families of monocular depth cues.
The geometry of learned concepts departs from a strictly sparse, quasi-orthogonal regime; representations show anisotropy aligned with task subspaces, positional information compresses into a ~2D subspace, and local neighborhoods remain connected even after removing position.
The paper proposes the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis (MRH), suggesting tokens are formed as convex mixtures of archetypes and activations form Minkowski sums of convex polytopes, implying concepts are convex regions rather than unbounded linear directions.
A dictionary of 32,000 visual concepts extracted via stable sparse autoencoders is released as an interactive visualization tool (DinoVision), providing a large-scale interpretability backbone.
The non-identifiability of Minkowski decomposition suggests that concept extraction cannot rely solely on final layer activations but must consider the sequence of transformations that formed them.
papers.limitation:
The evidence for the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis is observational and preliminary; multiple geometric hypotheses could generate similar patterns.
The analysis is model-specific (DINOv2-B) and conclusions are conditional on the dictionary, probes, and datasets used.
The work does not claim causal identification of concepts or their generative mechanisms.
future_direction: Developing structure-aware interpretability techniques that explain a layer through the sequence of transformations that formed it, rather than treating learned representations as opaque geometric objects.
Testing predictions of the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis, such as per-head block structure and subspace additivity across heads.
Exploring how to recover meaningful concept decompositions by leveraging intermediate representations like attention weights and earlier layer activations.
papers.abstract: DINOv2 is routinely deployed to recognize objects, scenes, and actions; yet the nature of what it perceives remains unknown. As a working baseline, we adopt the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) and operationalize it using SAEs, producing a 32,000-unit dictionary that serves as the interpretability backbone of our study, which unfolds in three parts. In the first part, we analyze how different downstream tasks recruit concepts from our learned dictionary, revealing functional specialization: classification exploits "Elsewhere" concepts that fire everywhere except on target objects, implementing learned negations; segmentation relies on boundary detectors forming coherent subspaces; depth estimation draws on three distinct monocular depth cues matching visual neuroscience principles. Following these functional results, we analyze the geometry and statistics of the concepts learned by the SAE. We found that representations are partly dense rather than strictly sparse. The dictionary evolves toward greater coherence and departs from maximally orthogonal ideals (Grassmannian frames). Within an image, tokens occupy a low dimensional, locally connected set persisting after removing position. These signs suggest representations are organized beyond linear sparsity alone. Synthesizing these observations, we propose a refined view: tokens are formed by combining convex mixtures of archetypes (e.g., a rabbit among animals, brown among colors, fluffy among textures). This structure is grounded in Gardenfors' conceptual spaces and in the model's mechanism as multi-head attention produces sums of convex mixtures, defining regions bounded by archetypes. We introduce the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis (MRH) and examine its empirical signatures and implications for interpreting vision-transformer representations.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: Modularity in Transformers: Investigating Neuron Separability & Specialization
papers.research_question: How modular and task-specialized are neurons in transformer models? The paper investigates the overlap and specialization of neurons across different tasks and data subsets.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence for task-specific neuron clusters in transformers, showing that neuron importance patterns are partially present even in randomly initialized models and are refined by training.
papers.conclusion: The methods reveal interpretable modularity in transformers, and the overlap between random and trained models provides evidence for a weak Lottery Ticket Hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific neuron clusters exist in transformers, with varying degrees of overlap between related tasks.
Neuron importance patterns persist to some extent even in randomly initialized models, suggesting an inherent structure that training refines.
MoEfication clusters correspond more strongly to task-specific neurons in earlier and later layers of the models.
For ViT, classes with intuitive similarities (e.g., 'insects' and 'non-insect invertebrates') show higher overlap in selected neurons.
For Mistral, unlearning a text subset (e.g., 'PubMed Central') leads to performance drops in related MMLU subjects (e.g., 'professional medicine').
papers.limitation:
We focused on MLP neurons and did not analyze attention mechanisms, which play a crucial role in transformer models.
Our analysis was limited to a specific set of tasks and datasets, and may not generalize to all domains or model architectures.
The interpretation of neuron importance and specialization is still somewhat qualitative and could benefit from more rigorous statistical analysis.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to include attention mechanisms and their interaction with MLP layers.
Developing more sophisticated clustering techniques that can capture hierarchical relationships between neurons and tasks.
Investigating how neuron specialization evolves during the training process.
papers.abstract: Transformer models are increasingly prevalent in various applications, yet our understanding of their internal workings remains limited. This paper investigates the modularity and task specialization of neurons within transformer architectures, focusing on both vision (ViT) and language (Mistral 7B) models. Using a combination of selective pruning and MoEfication clustering techniques, we analyze the overlap and specialization of neurons across different tasks and data subsets. Our findings reveal evidence of task-specific neuron clusters, with varying degrees of overlap between related tasks. We observe that neuron importance patterns persist to some extent even in randomly initialized models, suggesting an inherent structure that training refines. Additionally, we find that neuron clusters identified through MoEfication correspond more strongly to task-specific neurons in earlier and later layers of the models. This work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of transformer internals and offers insights into potential avenues for improving model interpretability and efficiency.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations
papers.research_question: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? How do transformers resolve the conflict between optimal Bayesian belief updating (a recursive process) and their parallelized, attention-driven architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. It explains why specific intermediate geometric structures emerge in transformer representations.
papers.conclusion: The geometric structures in transformer representations are a mathematical signature of how architectural constraints warp optimal Bayesian inference, revealing a precise interplay between theoretical necessity and implementation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating due to architectural constraints, bending optimal Bayesian inference into attention's parallelizable form.
The attention mechanism in the first layer implements a spectral algorithm that builds constrained beliefs, with attention weights approximating the decay of influence via eigenvalues of the data-generating transition matrix.
Intermediate representations (after attention) are fractals matching the constrained belief geometry, while final representations (after MLP) match the full, unconstrained belief geometry.
The attention pattern, OV vectors, and token embeddings can be theoretically predicted from the constrained belief updating equations.
For negative eigenvalues in the transition matrix (oscillatory dynamics), multiple attention heads are required to capture the full update pattern due to the non-negativity constraint of attention.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted on a tractable family of hidden Markov models (Mess3), which is a simplified setting.
As the HMM parameter α moves away from a central range, deviations between predicted and actual representations increase, and a complete characterization of these deviations remains for future work.
future_direction: A complete characterization of how deviations between predicted and actual representations scale with the HMM parameter α.
Applying the methodology to more complex cases, such as large language models trained on natural text, where the same tension between architecture and optimal inference is anticipated.
papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: On the Bias Against Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: How do inductive biases affect the performance of small to moderately-sized isotropic networks in unsupervised visual feature learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that inductive biases, such as locality in convolutions and distance preservation in continuous input encodings, significantly benefit small-scale isotropic networks for unsupervised visual learning, contrasting with large-scale models where these biases are removed.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that small-scale isotropic networks benefit from inductive biases, and improvements in small-scale models may transfer to large-scale models, enabling broader research participation.
papers.key_findings:
Convolutional networks outperform MLP-mixer and transformer networks in both unsupervised and classification tasks.
Continuous input encoding yields the best classification accuracy for a fixed unsupervised loss.
There is a strong correlation between unsupervised generative model performance and downstream classification accuracy.
Transformer models perform poorly on small-scale problems compared to convolutional and MLP-mixer models.
Different input encodings pair better with specific architecture types, suggesting untested inductive biases.
papers.limitation:
Limited computing resources prevent determining if poor transformer performance is due to data or architecture.
Linear probes were trained on isolated layers rather than combinations, which may not capture best features.
future_direction: Exploring linear probes on combinations of layers rather than isolated layers.
Investigating untested inductive biases that may improve large-scale isotropic networks.
papers.abstract: Borrowing from the transformer models that revolutionized the field of natural language processing, self-supervised feature learning for visual tasks has also seen state-of-the-art success using these extremely deep, isotropic networks. However, the typical AI researcher does not have the resources to evaluate, let alone train, a model with several billion parameters and quadratic self-attention activations. To facilitate further research, it is necessary to understand the features of these huge transformer models that can be adequately studied by the typical researcher. One interesting characteristic of these transformer models is that they remove most of the inductive biases present in classical convolutional networks. In this work, we analyze the effect of these and more inductive biases on small to moderately-sized isotropic networks used for unsupervised visual feature learning and show that their removal is not always ideal.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
